sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.summary: Introduces Chapter 5 on shallow foundations, covering scope, definitions, design philosophy, and applications. Defines shallow foundations (D/B < ~5), explains the two limit states controlling design (bearing capacity strength and settlement serviceability), and outlines the geotechnical investigation requirements needed to support bearing capacity and settlement analysis.
key_points: Shallow foundations are defined by a depth-to-width (D/B) ratio less than about 5; types include spread footings and mat foundations.
The primary geotechnical task is selecting an allowable bearing pressure, governed by two limit states: bearing capacity failure (strength) and settlement (serviceability).
Settlement controls the design for the majority of structures.
Field investigations must extend below the depth where stress change from foundations becomes negligible, and must provide parameters for both bearing capacity and settlement analysis.
Two design philosophies are used: Allowable Stress Design (ASD) and Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD); this chapter uses ASD.
Typical factors of safety against bearing capacity failure (FBC) range from 2 to 3 when bearing pressure is calculated using dead load and permanent live load.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever shallow foundations are being designed for any structure, as an orientation to the chapter's scope and methodology.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Defines the scope of Chapter 5, covering presumptive, empirical, and bearing capacity theory methods for shallow foundation design on soil and rock. Addresses special loading conditions (groundwater, uplift), special soil conditions (engineered fill, expansive/collapsing soils), and the geotechnical investigation requirements that must precede design.
sections.body:
This chapter describes design for shallow foundations, including presumptive and empirical methods, as well as those based on bearing capacity theory for soil and rock. Special loading conditions for shallow foundations are discussed, including the design of foundations and slabs below the groundwater level and resistance of uplift. This chapter also considers special soil conditions, such as foundations on engineered fill, foundations on expansive and collapsing soil and expansive rock, and foundations in other problem soils.

Shallow foundations can be defined as foundations with a depth to width (D/B) ratio less than about 5. Spread foundations transfer structural loads to the soil or rock over a relatively wide area and are usually synonymous with shallow foundations. Another type of shallow foundation is a mat foundation, in which the weight of the structure is distributed across the entire footprint of the structure. Most shallow foundations are constructed from reinforced, cast-in-place concrete. The interface between the shallow foundation and the soil or rock is referred to as the bearing surface and is located at the foundation bearing elevation. The bearing pressure is the stress imposed on the bearing surface by the foundation.

The primary geotechnical task for shallow foundation design is to select an allowable bearing pressure. This pressure is then used to size the foundations to support the anticipated structural loads. The allowable bearing pressure depends on two factors. First, an adequate factor of safety against ultimate bearing capacity failure must be provided. This is a strength limit state. Second, the settlements caused by changes in stress from the shallow foundations must not exceed the tolerances of the structure. This is a serviceability limit state. For the majority of structures, the design of shallow foundations is controlled by settlement, which is discussed in Chapter 5 of DM 7.1.

This chapter assumes that field investigations have been performed using sufficient in situ and laboratory testing to define the soil and/or rock stratigraphy as well as the groundwater conditions. For shallow foundations, the investigation should extend below the depth at which the change in stress imposed by the foundations is negligible (see Chapters 4 and 5 of DM 7.1). The investigation should provide the parameters required for bearing capacity and settlement analysis. Chapter 2 of DM 7.1 provides further information on field exploration while laboratory testing is discussed in Chapter 3 of that volume.
key_points: Chapter 5 covers presumptive, empirical, and bearing capacity theory methods for shallow foundations on soil and rock.
Shallow foundations have D/B < ~5; types include spread footings (also called footers/footings) and mat foundations.
The bearing surface is the interface between foundation and soil/rock at the foundation bearing elevation; bearing pressure is the stress at that surface.
Allowable bearing pressure selection depends on both a bearing capacity strength limit state and a settlement serviceability limit state.
Settlement controls design for most structures; see DM 7.1 Chapter 5 for settlement analysis.
Field investigations must characterize stratigraphy, groundwater, and provide parameters for bearing capacity and settlement analysis, extending to negligible stress-change depth.
sections.applicability: Applies at the start of any shallow foundation design project to establish the scope of required analyses and investigations.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Describes when shallow foundations are appropriate and what alternatives exist when they are not. Covers situations with compressible underlying soils (requiring deep foundations, ground improvement, or surcharging), thin layers of unsuitable soils (deepening footings or replacement with compacted fill), and foundations on rock (with guidance on managing differential settlement between rock and soil bearing areas).
sections.body:
Shallow foundations may be used at locations where suitable bearing soils are present within a few feet below the structure, provided that the stresses imposed by the foundation do not create unacceptable settlements.

Where suitable bearing soils are underlain by more compressible soils with depth and settlements are unacceptable, either deep foundations (see Chapter 6), ground improvement methods (see Chapter 1), or temporary surcharging (Chapter 5 of DM 7.1) may be required to bypass or modify the compressible soils. In some cases, shallow foundations can still be used if the bearing capacity of the near surface soils can be improved to allow smaller footings with higher bearing pressures. Construction of high quality compacted structural fill may also allow higher bearing pressures. In both cases, smaller footings will reduce stress penetration, which may reduce settlements.

Where a relatively thin layer of unsuitable loose or soft soil is present near the ground surface, it may be possible to deepen spread footings to suitable soils. Alternatively, the unsuitable soils can be excavated and replaced with higher quality compacted structural fill.

Shallow foundations may also be supported on rock. Where both rock and soil are found at bearing grade in different areas of a building, differential settlements may be of concern as discussed in Section 5-2.4.1. Over excavation of rock and replacement with a soil cushion between rock and the foundation may be required to reduce differential settlement.
key_points: Shallow foundations are suitable where competent bearing soils exist within a few feet of the surface and settlements are acceptable.
When compressible soils underlie suitable bearing soils, alternatives include deep foundations (Ch. 6), ground improvement (Ch. 1), or surcharging (DM 7.1 Ch. 5).
Improving near-surface bearing capacity allows smaller, higher-pressure footings that reduce stress penetration and potential settlements.
Thin unsuitable surface layers can be addressed by deepening footings or excavating and replacing with compacted structural fill.
Mixed rock-and-soil bearing grades create differential settlement risk; a soil cushion over rock may be needed to equalize settlements (see Section 5-2.4.1).
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating site suitability for shallow foundations and selecting between shallow foundation options or alternatives.

sections.title: Design Philosophy
sections.summary: Explains the two design philosophies for shallow foundations — Allowable Stress Design (ASD) and Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) — and establishes that this chapter uses ASD. Describes selection of the bearing capacity factor of safety (FBC), noting typical values of 2 to 3 for dead and permanent live load cases, with values depending on uncertainty and consequences of failure.
sections.body:
Two design philosophies are used to prevent bearing capacity failure of shallow foundations. Allowable stress design determines the ultimate bearing capacity of the soil and applies a factor of safety to determine an allowable bearing pressure. Load and resistance factor design (LRFD) uses load factors to account for uncertainties in loading conditions and resistance factors to accommodate uncertainty in resistance. The basis of the LRFD approach is discussed in Section 7-4.5. Settlement analysis is typically performed using unfactored loads, removing any difference between the two approaches.

Allowable stress design, which will be used in this chapter, requires the selection of a factor of safety against bearing capacity failure. The appropriate factor of safety, FBC, depends on the uncertainty of both the loading and the soil conditions, as well as the consequences of failure. Lower values of FBC are appropriate for well-defined conditions and low consequences, while higher FBC should be used for greater uncertainty and consequences. Typical values of FBC are in the range of 2 to 3 when the bearing pressure is calculated using dead load and permanent live load.
key_points: ASD divides ultimate bearing capacity by a factor of safety (FBC) to obtain allowable bearing pressure; LRFD uses load and resistance factors instead.
This chapter uses ASD; LRFD basis is discussed in Section 7-4.5.
Settlement analysis uses unfactored loads under both ASD and LRFD, eliminating practical differences between approaches for settlement.
FBC selection depends on loading uncertainty, soil condition uncertainty, and failure consequences.
Typical FBC values are 2 to 3 when bearing pressure is calculated from dead load plus permanent live load.
Lower FBC is appropriate for well-defined, low-consequence conditions; higher FBC for greater uncertainty or more severe consequences.
sections.applicability: Applies when establishing the design methodology and selecting an appropriate factor of safety for shallow foundation bearing capacity analysis.

sections.title: SHALLOW FOUNDATION DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS
sections.summary: Container section covering all major design considerations for shallow foundations, including foundation depth, gross/net bearing pressure, eccentricity, allowable bearing pressure, settlement, alternative support methods, and presumptive bearing pressures. Establishes the framework for the detailed subsections that follow.
key_points: Covers foundation depth requirements, bearing pressure definitions, eccentricity analysis, and allowable bearing pressure determination.
Introduces both gross and net bearing pressure concepts and their use in design.
Addresses eccentricity for rectangular and circular footings and limiting eccentricity criteria.
Provides a step-by-step procedure for determining allowable bearing pressure using bearing capacity and settlement checks.
Includes presumptive allowable bearing pressures for preliminary and lightly loaded structure design.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever shallow foundations are being designed or evaluated for any structure type.

sections.title: Foundation Depth
sections.summary: Specifies minimum depth requirements for individual footings, including placement below frost penetration depth, zones of high volume change, scour depths, and unsuitable materials such as organics, uncontrolled fills, and collapse-susceptible soils. Notes typical embedment of 12–18 inches where other constraints do not control.
sections.body:
In general, individual footings should be placed below: 1) the depth of frost penetration (see Chapter 1 of DM 7.1 for guidance or the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration website for site specific data), 2) zones of high volume change due to moisture fluctuations, and 3) scour depths for foundations in or adjacent to rivers and streams. Section 6-2.2.1 provides additional guidance for scour. Footings should extend to bear below organic materials, disturbed upper soils, uncontrolled fills, and zones of collapse-susceptible soils that are present. Alternatively, the unsuitable material should be removed and replaced with compacted structural fill.
Where other constraints do not control, shallow foundations on soil are typically embedded at least 12 to 18 inches. Some building codes specify minimum depth as a function of load.
key_points: Footings must be placed below frost penetration depth; site-specific data available from NOAA or DM 7.1 Chapter 1.
Footings must bear below zones of high volume change due to moisture, scour depths, organics, uncontrolled fills, and collapse-susceptible soils.
Unsuitable materials should be removed and replaced with compacted structural fill if bearing below them is not feasible.
Minimum embedment of 12–18 inches where no other constraints govern; some codes tie minimum depth to load magnitude.
sections.applicability: Applies to all shallow foundation designs where depth of placement must be established.

sections.title: Gross and Net Bearing Pressure
sections.summary: Defines gross and net bearing pressure for shallow foundations. Gross bearing pressure is the total load (structural load plus foundation weight plus overlying soil weight) divided by bearing area. Net bearing pressure subtracts the overburden pressure at bearing elevation, simplifying to structural load divided by area when soil and foundation unit weights are assumed equal.
sections.body:
The total load applied to the foundation bearing surface is the sum of the structural load (QDL+LL), the weight of the foundation (WF), and the weight of any overlying soil (WS). The gross bearing pressure applied to the soil by a shallow foundation is the total load divided by the area (A) of the bearing surface. The gross allowable bearing pressure is found as:

q_gross = (Q_DL+LL + W_F + W_S) / A   (5-1)

The net bearing pressure is sometimes used as a more convenient measure because it does not depend upon the weight of the foundation and overlying soil. The net bearing pressure is the gross bearing pressure minus the existing vertical overburden pressure at the foundation bearing elevation:

q_net = q_ult - sigma_zD   (5-2)

The unit weights of the foundation and soil backfill are typically assumed to be the same as the existing soil, which means that:

q_net = q_gross - sigma_zD ≈ (Q_DL+LL + W_F + W_S - W_F - W_S) / A = Q_DL+LL / A   (5-3)

Equation 5-3 defines the net bearing pressure only in terms of the structural load and foundation dimensions.
key_points: Gross bearing pressure = (structural load + foundation weight + overlying soil weight) / bearing area (Eq. 5-1).
Net bearing pressure = gross bearing pressure minus the existing vertical overburden at the bearing elevation (Eq. 5-2).
When foundation and backfill unit weights equal existing soil, net bearing pressure ≈ structural load / bearing area (Eq. 5-3).
Net bearing pressure is often more convenient as it eliminates dependence on foundation and soil weights.

equations.description: Gross bearing pressure: total load (structural load + foundation weight + overlying soil weight) divided by bearing area A.
Net bearing pressure: gross bearing pressure minus existing vertical overburden pressure at the foundation bearing elevation.
Net bearing pressure approximation when foundation and backfill unit weights equal existing soil unit weight; reduces to structural load divided by bearing area.

sections.applicability: Applies when calculating applied bearing pressures for shallow foundation design under vertical loading.

sections.title: Eccentricity
sections.summary: Covers eccentrically loaded shallow foundations subject to moments about one or both axes. Defines eccentricity, limiting criteria (middle-third rule for one-way and kern for two-way), corner bearing pressure equations, and the equivalent footing method (Meyerhof 1953) for ductile materials. Includes formulations for both rectangular and circular footings.
sections.body:
Shallow foundations may be eccentrically loaded by moments applied about one or both axes. The applied moments may be the result of either non-concentric vertical loading or directly applied to the foundation by the structure. The resulting eccentricity (e) is defined as the horizontal distance between the resultant force on the bearing surface and the centerlines of the foundation.

Eccentricity is calculated as:
e = M / Q   (5-4)
where:
M = applied moment and
Q = gross vertical load on the footing.

For cases where non-concentric vertical loading causes eccentricity, the applied moment can be determined by summing moments about the centerline of the footing. Where the eccentric loading is not aligned with the axes of the foundation, it is convenient to split the eccentricity into two parts and calculate eB and eL from the respective moments, MB and ML. By convention, the width (B) is the shorter dimension of the foundation, and the length (L) is the longer dimension.

Eccentricity causes an uneven bearing pressure. If the eccentricity is too high, the bearing pressure will no longer be compressive under all of the foundation. In order to prevent this, the eccentricity must be limited for normal loading. For eccentricity in one direction, the resultant must be in the middle one-third of the foundation:
eB ≤ B/6  or  eL ≤ L/6   (5-5)

For cases with eccentricity in two directions, the resultant must fall within a diamond-shaped area in the middle of the rectangular foundation called the kern and the following should be satisfied:
eB/B + eL/L ≤ 1/6   (5-6)

If the eccentricity falls within these limits, the bearing pressure at the four corners of the rectangular foundation can be found as:
q_corner = q_gross * (1 ± 6*eB/B ± 6*eL/L)   (5-7)

The maximum value, qmax, should be used for comparisons with ultimate bearing capacity for brittle materials such as sensitive soil and rock. For more ductile materials, it is appropriate to approximate the applied bearing pressure using the equivalent footing method (Meyerhof 1953). The equivalent footing is the bearing area on which the resultant bearing force is centered. The equivalent width (B') and length (L') are calculated as:
B' = B - 2*eB   (5-8)
L' = L - 2*eL   (5-9)

The equivalent uniform bearing pressure for a rectangular foundation can be found as:
q_unif = (Q_LL+DL + W_F + W_S) / (B' * L')   (5-10)

Circular footings can only have eccentricity in one direction. The resultant is centered on the lens-shaped area circumscribed by two arcs. If the aspect ratio of the equivalent rectangle is the same as the circumscribed area, then the equivalent dimensions can be calculated as:
L' = a'b' = 2*sqrt(r^2 - e_x^2) / (1 - (e_x/r)^2) * arccos(e_x/r) ... [see Eq. 5-11 in source]
B' = b'c' = B' / L' * sqrt(r^2 - e_x^2) ... [see Eq. 5-12 in source]
where ex = eccentricity and r = radius of the foundation. Note that the inverse cosine term in Eq. 5-11 must be expressed in radians.
key_points: Eccentricity e = M/Q, where M is applied moment and Q is gross vertical load (Eq. 5-4).
For one-way eccentricity, resultant must be within middle third: eB ≤ B/6 or eL ≤ L/6 (Eq. 5-5).
For two-way eccentricity, resultant must fall within the kern: eB/B + eL/L ≤ 1/6 (Eq. 5-6).
Corner bearing pressures for rectangular footings given by Eq. 5-7; qmax used for brittle materials.
Equivalent footing method (Meyerhof 1953) uses reduced dimensions B'=B-2eB and L'=L-2eL for ductile materials (Eqs. 5-8, 5-9).
Circular footings have eccentricity in one direction only; equivalent rectangle dimensions given by Eqs. 5-11 and 5-12.

equations.description: Eccentricity: e = M/Q, where M is the applied moment and Q is the gross vertical load on the footing.
Middle-third rule for one-way eccentricity: eB ≤ B/6 or eL ≤ L/6, ensuring compressive bearing pressure across full foundation width or length.
Kern criterion for two-way eccentricity: eB/B + eL/L ≤ 1/6, ensuring resultant falls within kern of rectangular foundation.
Corner bearing pressure for rectangular foundation under two-way eccentricity: q_corner = q_gross*(1 ± 6eB/B ± 6eL/L).
Equivalent footing width for eccentric loading on rectangular foundation: B' = B - 2*eB.
Equivalent footing length for eccentric loading on rectangular foundation: L' = L - 2*eL.
Equivalent uniform bearing pressure for eccentrically loaded rectangular foundation using reduced equivalent dimensions B' and L'.
Equivalent length L' of rectangular area for eccentrically loaded circular footing, expressed in terms of eccentricity ex and radius r; inverse cosine in radians.
Equivalent width B' of rectangular area for eccentrically loaded circular footing, expressed in terms of eccentricity ex, radius r, and equivalent length L'.

sections.applicability: Applies when shallow foundations are subjected to moments or non-concentric vertical loads, requiring eccentricity analysis and bearing pressure distribution checks.

sections.title: Allowable Bearing Pressure
sections.summary: Describes the step-by-step procedure for determining allowable bearing pressure (qall): calculate ultimate bearing capacity, apply a factor of safety to obtain gross and net allowable bearing pressures (Eqs. 5-13, 5-14), check settlement, and reduce bearing pressure if settlement criteria are not met. Design may be controlled by either bearing capacity or settlement.
sections.body:
The allowable bearing pressure (qall) is the highest bearing pressure that meets the design requirements for both factored bearing capacity and settlement. In a general sense, the allowable bearing pressure can be determined using the following steps:
1) Calculate the ultimate bearing capacity (qult) using the methods in Section 5-3.
2) Apply an appropriate factor of safety (FBC) to the ultimate bearing capacity. In some cases, it may be appropriate to start with a presumptive allowable bearing pressure from Section 5-2.5 rather than factoring a calculated bearing capacity.
   a. The gross allowable bearing pressure is found as:
      q_all,gross = q_ult / F_BC   (5-13)
   b. The net allowable bearing pressure is found as (Peck et al. 1974):
      q_all,net ≤ q_ult/F_BC - sigma_zD   (5-14)
3) Calculate settlement using foundations sized according to q_all,net.
   a. If the total, differential, and distortion settlement criteria are met, then the net allowable bearing pressure from Equation 5-14 can be used and the design is controlled by the bearing capacity.
   b. If not, reduce the bearing pressure until the settlement criteria are met. The reduced value is the net allowable bearing pressure that should be used for design. The design is controlled by settlement.
Once an allowable bearing pressure has been determined, it is compared to the calculated bearing pressure. Either net or gross pressures can be used, as appropriate. The foundation dimensions are adjusted to obtain an applied bearing pressure less than, but not greatly exceeding, the allowable value. This process is often iterative.
key_points: Allowable bearing pressure is the highest value satisfying both bearing capacity and settlement criteria.
Gross allowable bearing pressure: q_all,gross = q_ult / F_BC (Eq. 5-13).
Net allowable bearing pressure: q_all,net ≤ q_ult/F_BC - sigma_zD (Eq. 5-14, after Peck et al. 1974).
Settlement must be checked after sizing foundations to q_all,net; design may be settlement-controlled.
Foundation sizing is iterative; applied pressure should be less than but not greatly exceed allowable.

equations.description: Gross allowable bearing pressure: q_all,gross = q_ult / F_BC, where F_BC is the bearing capacity factor of safety.
Net allowable bearing pressure: q_all,net ≤ q_ult/F_BC - sigma_zD, subtracting overburden pressure from factored ultimate capacity (Peck et al. 1974).

sections.applicability: Applies to all shallow foundation designs requiring determination of an allowable bearing pressure considering both bearing capacity and settlement.

sections.title: Settlement Considerations
sections.summary: Addresses settlement-related design issues for shallow foundations, including strategies to equalize differential settlement under variable column loads, handling transitions between soil and rock bearing at the same elevation, and techniques such as over-excavation/compacted fill or grade beams to mitigate differential settlement.
sections.body:
Settlement constraints govern the design of many shallow foundations and should be carefully considered prior to a comprehensive consideration of bearing capacity. Chapter 5 of DM 7.1 provides detailed instructions for settlement calculations. Some additional considerations specific to shallow foundations are considered in this section.

Some structures have widely varying column or wall loads that have the potential to cause problematic differential settlement. In this case, q_all,net can be varied in attempt to equalize settlements. Often this requires using a lower bearing pressure and larger footings to support the heavier column loads. If the settlement prone soils are shallow, it may also be possible to increase the q_all,net for the heavily loaded footings by excavating poor soils and replacing with high-quality compacted structural fill along an interior line of columns.

At some sites, the depth to rock varies widely and both rock and soil may be found at the bearing elevation. In this case, differential settlements will be a concern, because of the dissimilar settlement characteristics of soil and rock. The choice of an appropriate solution will be informed by both the extent of the dissimilar bearing condition and the relative flexibility of the supported structure. One procedure that may be used to reduce differential settlement is to over excavate the rock where footings are located and backfill with compacted structural fill. The compacted structural fill should be designed to compress such that differential settlements are no longer a concern. Typically, the fill is clay placed with a lower relative compaction criterion, such as to 90 percent of maximum dry density. A thickness of one to two feet of this type of material will usually improve the differential settlement characteristics. The length of the transition zone required to mitigate differential settlement will depend on the flexibility of the structure. Section 5-6.1 further describes procedures for shallow foundations on fill.

Alternatively, a deepened footing can be reinforced as a grade beam that can allow the differential settlement to be distributed over a longer span. In other cases, it may be most economical to use shallow foundations bearing on rock for most of the structure along with deep foundations and grade beams at the locations where the rock is deeper.
key_points: Settlement often governs shallow foundation design and should be evaluated before detailed bearing capacity analysis.
Varying q_all,net across footings can equalize differential settlement under variable column loads.
When rock and soil coexist at bearing elevation, over-excavation of rock and backfilling with compacted clay fill (≈90% max dry density, 1–2 ft thick) can reduce differential settlement.
Grade beams reinforced over deepened footings can distribute differential settlement over a longer span.
DM 7.1 Chapter 5 provides detailed settlement calculation procedures.
sections.applicability: Applies when shallow foundations bear on variable soils or mixed soil/rock conditions where differential settlement is a design concern.

sections.title: Alternative Methods of Supporting Shallow Spread Foundations
sections.summary: Describes alternatives to individual shallow footings for sites with highly compressible soils, including mat foundations, increased embedment depth, soil replacement with compacted fill, turned-down edge foundations, and ground improvement techniques such as rigid inclusion piers, aggregate piers, vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, soil mixing, and preloading with wick drains.
sections.body:
For sites with highly compressible soils, very low bearing pressures may be required to meet the settlement criteria. As the size of isolated foundations becomes large, the use of a mat foundation should be considered (see Section 5-4).

Other alternatives to individual shallow foundations are available. If stronger or less compressible soils are present, the foundation depth may be increased to reach suitable bearing soils. Another alternative is to excavate and replace unsuitable soils with compacted structural fill for individual column footings, or in strips along column lines. Turned down edge foundations integral with the floor slab may be used for lightly loaded structures. Many of the site improvement techniques discussed in Chapter 1 are suitable to improve bearing capacity and reduce settlement for shallow foundations. Some of these techniques work by transferring load to a suitable bearing stratum while others densify the soil, reducing settlement potential. Useful techniques for shallow foundations include rigid inclusion piers, aggregate piers, vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, soil mixing methods, and preloading with or without wick drains to facilitate improved drainage.
key_points: When isolated footings become very large due to low allowable pressures, transition to mat foundation (Section 5-4).
Increasing embedment depth, soil excavation/replacement, and turned-down slab edges are alternatives to spread footings.
Ground improvement techniques include rigid inclusion piers, aggregate piers, vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, soil mixing, and preloading with wick drains.
Some ground improvement methods transfer load to stronger strata; others densify soil to reduce settlement potential.
sections.applicability: Applies at sites with highly compressible or unsuitable soils where standard shallow spread foundations cannot economically meet bearing capacity or settlement criteria.

sections.title: Presumptive Allowable Bearing Pressure
sections.summary: Provides guidance on the use of presumptive allowable bearing pressures (Table 5-1) without formal bearing capacity or settlement calculations. Covers appropriate use cases (preliminary estimates, lightly loaded structures, rock foundations), materials for which presumptive values should not be used, and criteria for adjacent footing spacing to prevent overlapping stress zones.
sections.body:
Presumptive bearing pressures are selected without formal calculation of bearing capacity and/or settlement. They are sometimes used to estimate allowable bearing pressures (qall) for: 1) preliminary estimates for any project, 2) design values for lightly loaded structures, or 3) design values for foundations on rock materials where detailed analysis is unnecessary due to the relatively high bearing capacity of the rock. Presumptive bearing pressures should not be used for foundations on normally consolidated clays, organic soils, or uncontrolled fills.

Table 5-1 lists presumptive allowable bearing pressures for a variety of rock and soil types. These presumptive qall values are intended to provide a reasonable safety factor against ultimate failure and to avoid detrimental total and differential settlements of individual footings for footings subjected to vertical loads. The effects of eccentricity on bearing pressure should be considered when using presumptive qall. Presumptive qall values for soils should be used with caution and verified by performance of nearby structures founded on similar density or consistency material. Bearing strata underlain by a weaker material can be considered using presumptive bearing pressures and the method illustrated in Figure 5-2.

When presumptive qall are used in lieu of bearing capacity analysis, it may still be appropriate to check settlement. The zones of induced stresses from adjacent foundations should not overlap within a depth of 2B below square footings or 4B below continuous footings because of settlement concerns. In order to accomplish this, lines projected downward from adjacent footings at angle of 30° from the vertical should not intersect within these depths.
key_points: Presumptive bearing pressures are used without formal calculation for preliminary estimates, lightly loaded structures, or rock foundations.
Must NOT be used for normally consolidated clays, organic soils, or uncontrolled fills.
Table 5-1 provides presumptive qall for rock and soil types; values include built-in safety factors against failure and detrimental settlement.
Eccentricity effects on bearing pressure must still be considered when using presumptive qall.
Stress zones from adjacent footings should not overlap within 2B (square) or 4B (continuous) depth; use 30° projection lines to check.
Settlement check may still be appropriate even when presumptive qall are used in lieu of bearing capacity analysis.
figures: Figure 5-2 — Bearing strata underlain by weaker material evaluated using presumptive bearing pressures
tables: Table 5-1 — Presumptive Allowable Bearing Pressures (B > 3 ft) (after NRCS 2022, Das 2022)
sections.applicability: Applies when formal bearing capacity and settlement calculations are not required or appropriate, particularly for preliminary design or foundations on rock.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity of Soil and Rock
sections.summary: Container section introducing the bearing capacity of soil and rock topic, covering ultimate bearing capacity theory including general shear, local shear, and punching shear failure modes as developed by Terzaghi (1943) and subsequent researchers. Sets the stage for subsections on shear strength selection and calculation methods.
sections.body:
The ultimate bearing capacity can be defined as the highest applied stress that the soil or rock withstands at the point of plastic failure. As developed by Terzaghi (1943), ultimate bearing capacity considers two types of failure.

General shear failure occurs along a well-defined failure surface below and beyond the edges of a footing as shown in Figure 5-3(a). The triangular Zone I under the footing in Figure 5-3 acts as though it is part of the footing, and the soil remains in an elastic state. For a vertical load, the major principal stress is aligned vertically in Zone I. In Zone III, the soil reaches a state of Rankine passive earth pressure with the major principal stress aligned horizontally. Zone II is known as the zone of radial shear, which allows the stress system to rotate between Zones I and III.

General shear failure normally occurs in a dense coarse-grained or very stiff cohesive soil. At failure, the soil on both sides of the footing bulges and the footing may rotate. A state of plastic equilibrium is reached in Zones II and III in this type of failure. General shear failure can be catastrophic for large mat supported structures although individual footings rarely experience this type of failure. Dense and very stiff soils generally experience relatively low settlements at typical allowable bearing pressures.

Local shear failure occurs when the soil in Zone II compresses rather than developing a plastic shear state as shown in Figure 5-3(b). For this reason, the soil in Zone III is not engaged in the failure mechanism. Individual shear failure surfaces typically do not reach the ground surface. Failure is not sudden, and tilting does not occur. Settlements are usually substantial, and plastic equilibrium is only partially developed.

As shown in Figure 5-3(c), the dense or stiff soils associated with general shear failure develop qult at low strain or settlement. The ultimate bearing capacity is well-defined. In contrast, the local shear mechanism in loose or soft soils results in large strains and settlements. Because much of the movement is associated with the compressibility of the soil, the magnitude of qult is much less distinct.

Punching shear is dominated by compression of the soil below and vertical shear along the sides of the footing (Vesic 1973). Little to no movement occurs in the soil adjacent to the footing. Considerations of settlement will control when punching shear is the dominant bearing capacity failure mode. The term punching shear is also used by some to refer to the case of a footing punching through a thin layer of stiff consistency or dense soil into a soft consistency or loose soil below. This mechanism is discussed in Section 5-3.6.

As indicated by Figure 5-3(d), the general shear mechanism applies mostly to dense soils at relatively shallow depths. At lower relative densities and greater footing depths, the failure mode transitions through local failure to punching shear. The bearing capacity theories discussed in Section 5-3.1.2 assume a general shear failure mechanism. Methods to account for local shear are discussed in Section 5-3.1.3.
key_points: Ultimate bearing capacity is the highest applied stress the soil/rock withstands at plastic failure (Terzaghi 1943).
General shear failure: well-defined failure surface, dense/stiff soils, plastic equilibrium in Zones II & III; can be catastrophic for mat-supported structures.
Local shear failure: Zone II compresses rather than shearing, failure surfaces don't reach the surface, substantial settlements, qult less distinct.
Punching shear: dominated by compression below and vertical shear along footing sides; settlement governs design in this mode.
Failure mode depends on relative density and depth; transitions from general shear (dense, shallow) to local/punching (loose, deep).
Bearing capacity theories in Section 5-3.1.2 assume general shear; local shear corrections are in Section 5-3.1.3.

sections.applicability: Applies when selecting an appropriate bearing capacity failure mode assumption for foundation design in any soil type.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Theory
sections.summary: Container section for bearing capacity theory, encompassing the three failure modes (general shear, local shear, punching shear) and their relationship to soil density and footing depth. References subsections for shear strength selection, ultimate bearing capacity calculation, and local shear correction methods.
key_points: Three failure modes: general shear, local shear, and punching shear, each governed by different soil and geometry conditions.
General shear is the basis for the standard bearing capacity equations; local shear and punching require corrections.
Failure mode transitions with relative density and footing depth as shown in Figure 5-3(d).
figures: Figure 5-3
sections.applicability: Applies as the parent section introducing all bearing capacity theory topics for soil and rock foundations.

sections.title: Shear Strength for Bearing Capacity Analysis
sections.summary: Describes how to select appropriate shear strength parameters (drained effective stress vs. undrained total stress) for bearing capacity analyses based on soil type, drainage characteristics, and loading conditions. Covers clean sands/gravels (effective stress only), fine-grained soils (undrained at end of construction, possibly drained long-term), and parameter selection for saturated vs. unsaturated soils.
sections.body:
Bearing capacity is controlled by the shear strength of the soil. The type of shear strength parameters used in bearing capacity analyses depends on the field loading condition, soil type, and groundwater level. Loads are typically applied to foundations over a period of time, such as when a building or a bridge is under construction. This loading condition may represent drained or undrained loading depending on the type of soil being loaded and the length of time required to apply the load.

In clean sands and gravels, drainage is almost instantaneous and does not practically depend on how long it takes to build the structure. These soils only require effective stress analysis unless dynamic loading is anticipated. If substantial fines are present, the possibility of developing an undrained condition should be considered.

In contrast, substantial time is required for excess pore pressures to dissipate in fine-grained soils after loading. These soils usually require undrained analysis for conditions at the end of loading as well as for any rapid or dynamic loading. In some cases, long-term effective stress conditions should also be checked. For example, the drained bearing capacity of heavily overconsolidated clays often controls the design.

Laboratory and field testing methods to determine shear strength parameters for most soil types are summarized in the Prologue. For bearing capacity analysis, effective strength parameters (φʹ, cʹ) should be used for long-term conditions in all soil types. For saturated fine-grained soils, the use of undrained shear strength (su) with φ = 0 is appropriate. Undrained shear strength parameters (φ, c) should be used for unsaturated soils with low permeability, including coarse-grained soils with substantial fines.
key_points: Shear strength parameter selection depends on soil type, drainage, and loading rate/duration.
Clean sands and gravels: effective stress analysis (φʹ, cʹ); undrained conditions rarely govern unless fines are substantial or dynamic loading is present.
Fine-grained soils: undrained analysis (su, φ=0) required at end of construction; long-term drained analysis may also control, especially for heavily overconsolidated clays.
Effective strength parameters (φʹ, cʹ) apply to all soil types for long-term drained conditions.
Undrained shear strength su with φ=0 is appropriate for saturated fine-grained soils.
Unsaturated low-permeability soils (including coarse-grained with substantial fines) use total stress undrained parameters (φ, c).
sections.applicability: Applies when determining which shear strength parameters to use as input to bearing capacity calculations for any soil type or loading condition.

sections.title: Calculation of Ultimate Bearing Capacity
sections.summary: Presents the general bearing capacity equation framework with three superimposed resistance terms (cohesion, surcharge, soil weight), each with a corresponding bearing capacity factor (Nc, Nq, Nγ) and correction factors (Ψc, Ψq, Ψγ). Provides three forms of the equation for drained, undrained unsaturated, and undrained saturated conditions. References Terzaghi, Meyerhof, Brinch Hansen, and Vesic methods with factors tabulated in Table 5-2 and plotted in Figure 5-5.
sections.body:
Bearing capacity is a complex phenomenon that cannot be modeled exactly. Multiple equations have been developed to estimate the ultimate bearing capacity of soil. These equations are based on the upper and lower bound theorems of plasticity and include the work of Prandtl (1920), Terzaghi (1943), Meyerhof (1951), Brinch Hansen (1970), and Vesic (1973, 1975). In their basic form, the equations apply to general shear failure below a continuous strip footing of width, B, with soil shear strength governed by the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion. The basic bearing capacity solutions also assume vertical loading, a horizontal bearing surface, foundation depth less than the width, and a horizontal ground surface. Methods to address other variations of these factors are discussed in Section 5-3.3.

In most methods, the bearing capacity problem is simplified by replacing the soil above the bearing elevation with an equivalent surcharge as shown in Figure 5-4(a). This conservatively neglects the shear strength of the soil above the foundation depth. Alternatively, Meyerhof (1951) assumed that the failure surface continued to the ground surface and replaced the triangular wedge with equivalent stresses, p0 and s0. Meyerhof's geometry is shown in Figure 5-4(b). Basic formulations also assume that the groundwater table is deeper than the failure zone.

With these assumptions, the bearing capacity problem can be separated into three distinct terms or superimposed sources of bearing resistance. The first term is connected to the cohesion (or undrained shear strength) along the failure surface and has a bearing capacity factor, Nc. The second term is related to the surcharge and has a bearing capacity factor, Nq. The third term is related to the weight of the soil above the failure surface and has a bearing capacity factor, Nγ.

For effective stress or drained analysis, the ultimate bearing capacity of the soil is given by Eq. 5-15.

For undrained conditions in unsaturated soils, the ultimate bearing capacity is given by Eq. 5-16.

For undrained conditions in saturated soils, the ultimate bearing capacity is given by Eq. 5-17.

The bearing capacity factors depend on the friction angle of the soil because it controls the shape of the failure surface. Three methods are provided herein to determine the bearing capacity factors. The values are provided in Table 5-2 for the Terzaghi (1943), Meyerhof (1951), and Brinch Hansen (1970) methods. The factors provided by Vesic (1973) are nearly identical to those proposed by Meyerhof and Hansen. The factors can also be determined from the plots or equations provided in Figure 5-5.

Various studies have compared the bearing capacity methods to full-scale loading test data (e.g. Milovic 1965, Bowles 1996). The comparisons focused on foundations with Df/B less than one and L/B less than four. Recommendations for the suitability of the various methods are provided in Table 5-3.
key_points: Three superimposed resistance terms: cohesion (Nc), surcharge (Nq), and soil weight (Nγ), each multiplied by correction factors (Ψc, Ψq, Ψγ).
Eq. 5-15 applies for drained/effective stress conditions using cʹ, φʹ, and effective stresses.
Eq. 5-16 applies for undrained conditions in unsaturated soils using total stress parameters (c, φ) and total stresses.
Eq. 5-17 applies for undrained saturated soils using su and φ=0; the Nγ and Nq terms drop out.
Bearing capacity factors Nc, Nq, Nγ depend on friction angle; values tabulated in Table 5-2 for Terzaghi, Meyerhof, and Brinch Hansen; Vesic factors are nearly identical to Meyerhof/Hansen.
Basic equations assume general shear, strip footing, vertical load, horizontal bearing surface, Df < B, and GWT below failure zone.
Method suitability based on full-scale load test comparisons (Df/B < 1, L/B < 4) is given in Table 5-3.

equations.description: Ultimate bearing capacity for drained (effective stress) conditions: qult = cʹ·Nc·Ψc + σʹzD·Nq·Ψq + 0.5·γ·B·Nγ·Ψγ, where cʹ is effective cohesion, σʹzD is effective vertical stress at bearing elevation, γ is average effective unit weight between Df and Df+B, and Nc, Nq, Nγ are bearing capacity factors depending on φʹ.

Ultimate bearing capacity for undrained conditions in unsaturated soils: qult = c·Nc·Ψc + σzD·Nq·Ψq + 0.5·γ·B·Nγ·Ψγ, using undrained cohesion c, undrained friction angle φ, total unit weight γ, and total vertical stress σzD at bearing elevation.

Ultimate bearing capacity for undrained conditions in saturated soils (φ=0): qult = su·Nc·Ψc + σzD·Ψq, where su is undrained shear strength, σzD is total vertical stress at bearing elevation, and Nc is the bearing capacity factor for φ=0.
