sections.applicability: Applies when calculating ultimate bearing capacity of a continuous strip footing under drained or undrained conditions using the general shear failure mechanism.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Corrections for Local and Punching Shear
sections.summary: Describes methods to correct bearing capacity calculations when local or punching shear failure governs instead of general shear. Covers three approaches: constant shear strength reduction (Terzaghi), variable reduction based on relative density (Vesic), and compressibility factors based on rigidity index (Vesic). Notes that settlement typically controls allowable bearing pressure in these cases.
sections.body: As noted in the introduction to this section, the bearing capacity theories assume a general shear failure mode, which is only appropriate for dense and/or stiff soils. For most soils, a local or punching shear mechanism is more appropriate. In these cases, settlement considerations will almost always control the allowable bearing pressure and an accurate determination of the ultimate bearing capacity is less important. A variety of methods to approximate local shear have been proposed. A few of the more common approaches are summarized in Table 5-4.
key_points: General shear failure assumption is only appropriate for dense and/or stiff soils; local or punching shear governs for most soils.
Settlement considerations almost always control allowable bearing pressure when local/punching shear governs, making exact qult less critical.
Terzaghi (1943) constant reduction: c* = 0.67c', φ* = tan⁻¹(0.67 tan φ'). May be too conservative for sands and potentially unsafe in some cases.
Vesic (1973) variable reduction ties reduction factor R to relative density Dr, allowing transitional behavior between local and general shear.
Vesic (1973) compressibility factors based on rigidity index provide an alternative approach using footing dimensions, soil properties, and stress conditions.
sections.applicability: Applies when bearing capacity analysis is performed for loose or soft soils where local or punching shear failure mode is more appropriate than general shear.

sections.title: Groundwater Correction
sections.summary: Explains when and how to apply groundwater corrections in bearing capacity calculations. Correction is required when the groundwater table is within one footing width below the bearing elevation, and applies only to drained (effective stress) analyses. Groundwater effect is handled by modifying the unit weight used in calculations, with three possible cases shown in Figure 5-6 under hydrostatic conditions.
sections.body: Groundwater correction is required when the groundwater table is higher than one footing width below the bearing elevation. Groundwater correction is only required for drained (effective stress) analysis. Groundwater is considered by changing the unit weight used in the bearing capacity calculations. The three possible cases are shown in Figure 5-6. These cases assume hydrostatic conditions (i.e., no seepage forces exist).
key_points: Groundwater correction is required when GWT is shallower than one footing width (B) below the bearing elevation.
Correction applies only to drained (effective stress) analyses; undrained analyses are not affected.
The correction is implemented by modifying the unit weight used in bearing capacity equations.
Three possible GWT cases are defined (see Figure 5-6), all assuming hydrostatic conditions with no seepage forces.
figures: Figure 5-6
sections.applicability: Applies when performing drained bearing capacity analysis and the groundwater table is located at or above a depth equal to one footing width below the foundation bearing elevation.

sections.title: Methods to Account for Complicating Effects
sections.summary: Introduces correction factors for bearing capacity complications not covered in basic solutions: foundation shape, depth, load inclination, base inclination, and ground inclination. Explains that lumped correction factors (Ψc, Ψq, Ψγ) are products of individual effect factors, and warns that correction factors cannot be mixed across methods. Addresses eccentricity via equivalent dimensions B′ and L′.
sections.body:
Multiple aspects of a foundation design can affect the bearing capacity that are not included in the basic solutions presented in Section 5-3.1.2. These include foundation shape and depth, load inclination, base inclination, and ground inclination. A shallow foundation with all three inclinations is illustrated in Figure 5-7.

The correction methods in the following sections are based on both theoretical considerations and empirical evidence. For this reason, the correction factors cannot usually be applied across methods, i.e., Meyerhof corrections should be used only with the Meyerhof bearing capacity factors. In addition, care should be taken combining many corrections within a given method. If bearing capacity controls a design with multiple complicating factors, numerical analysis is likely warranted. Limit equilibrium slope stability analysis can be used to analyze strip foundations on slopes.

Lumped correction factors for complicating effects (Ψc, Ψq, and Ψγ) were included in Eqn. 5-15 to 5-17. In most cases, these factors are found by multiplying factors for individual effects, such that:

Ψc = sc · dc · ic · bc · gc  (5-18)
Ψq = sq · dq · iq · bq · gq  (5-19)
Ψγ = sγ · dγ · iγ · bγ · gγ  (5-20)

where:
sc, sq, sγ = shape factors,
dc, dq, dγ = depth factors,
ic, iq, iγ = load inclination factors,
bc, bq, bγ = sloping base factors, and
gc, gq, gγ = sloping ground factors.

As discussed in Section 5-2.3, foundations are sometime eccentrically loaded. Eccentricity affects the bearing capacity as well as the bearing pressure. The most common approach is to use the equivalent dimensions, B′ and L′ (Eqn. 5-8 and 5-9), to determine the shape factors. The B′ dimension should also be used in the Nγ term to calculate bearing capacity. Conservatively, the actual dimensions should be used to calculate the depth factors.
key_points: Complicating effects not in basic solutions include shape, depth, load inclination, base inclination, and ground inclination.
Correction factors are method-specific; Meyerhof factors must only be used with Meyerhof bearing capacity factors.
Lumped correction factors Ψc, Ψq, Ψγ are products of shape (s), depth (d), inclination (i), base (b), and ground (g) factors.
When many corrections are needed and bearing capacity controls design, numerical analysis is likely warranted.
Eccentricity is handled via equivalent dimensions B′ and L′ for shape factors and Nγ term; actual dimensions used conservatively for depth factors.
Limit equilibrium slope stability analysis can be used for strip foundations on slopes.

equations.description: Lumped correction factor for cohesion term: Ψc = sc · dc · ic · bc · gc
Lumped correction factor for surcharge term: Ψq = sq · dq · iq · bq · gq
Lumped correction factor for unit weight term: Ψγ = sγ · dγ · iγ · bγ · gγ

figures: Figure 5-7
sections.applicability: Applies when shallow foundation bearing capacity calculations must account for shape, depth, load inclination, base inclination, or ground inclination effects beyond the basic strip footing solution.

sections.title: Terzaghi (1943) Method
sections.summary: Describes the Terzaghi upper bound bearing capacity method's approach to complicating effects, which considers shape as the only correction factor. Shape factors for continuous, square, and circular foundations are tabulated in Table 5-5. All other correction factors (depth, inclination, base, ground) are set to 1 in the lumped factor equations.
sections.body: Shape is the only complicating factor considered by the Terzaghi upper bound method. The factors are listed in Table 5-5. In some cases, interpolation can be used between the shape factors for square and continuous foundations. The other factors should be set equal to 1 in Eqn. 5-18 to 5-20.
key_points: Terzaghi's method only accounts for foundation shape as a complicating factor; all other correction factors (depth, inclination, etc.) are set to 1.
Shape factors are tabulated for continuous (sc=1, sq=1, sγ=1), square (sc=1.3, sq=1, sγ=0.8), and circular (sc=1.3, sq=1, sγ=0.6) foundations.
Interpolation between square and continuous shape factors is permitted for rectangular foundations.
All non-shape factors in Eqn. 5-18 to 5-20 must be set to 1 when using the Terzaghi method.
sections.applicability: Applies when using the Terzaghi (1943) upper bound bearing capacity method to correct for foundation shape (continuous, square, or circular).

sections.title: Meyerhof (1963) Method
sections.summary: Summarizes the Meyerhof (1963) bearing capacity correction factors for shape, depth, and load inclination, tabulated in Table 5-6. Notes that shape factors reduce to 1 under inclined loading per experimental evidence, and that Meyerhof did not provide base or ground inclination factors — instead offering a separate sloping-ground solution covered in Section 5-3.4.
sections.body:
Meyerhof (1963) presents shape, depth, and load inclination factors, which are summarized in Table 5-6. The laboratory experiments used to develop the inclination factors indicated that the shape factors tend toward one under inclined load. In other words, it is safe to assume that sc = sq = sγ = 1 if load inclination is present.

Meyerhof (1963) did not provide base or inclination factors in this form. Meyerhof developed a separate solution for sloping ground that is discussed briefly in Section 5-3.4.
key_points: Meyerhof (1963) provides shape, depth, and load inclination correction factors; base and ground inclination factors are not included.
Under inclined loading, shape factors revert to 1 (sc = sq = sγ = 1); do not combine shape and inclined load factors.
For φ > 10°, shape factors use the passive pressure coefficient KP = tan²(π/4 + φ′/2).
Depth factors for φ = 0: dc = 1 + 0.2·k·(KP)^0.5, dq = dγ = 1; for φ′ > 10°: dq = dγ = 1 + 0.1·k·(KP)^0.5.
Inclination factors: ic = iq = (1 – 2θ/π)², iγ = (1 – θ/φ′)², where θ = tan⁻¹(H/V) in radians.
Sloping ground is handled by a separate Meyerhof solution discussed in Section 5-3.4.
sections.applicability: Applies when using the Meyerhof (1963) bearing capacity method and correcting for foundation shape, embedment depth, and/or inclined loading conditions.

sections.title: Brinch Hansen (1970) Method
sections.summary: Describes the Brinch Hansen (1970) correction factor framework, which handles the most complicating effects of any method: shape, depth, load inclination, base inclination, and ground inclination. For φ = 0 the lumped Nc correction factor is additive (Eq. 5-21) rather than multiplicative. Three options address missing Nc factors for drained/unsaturated conditions. Load direction must be considered for inclination factors on rectangular foundations.
sections.body:
The Brinch Hansen (1970) method allows the most complicating factors to be considered. For this reason, it is more complex than the other methods. Similar to Meyerhof, the shape factors are adjusted for inclined loading.

Brinch Hansen considered conditions for undrained shear strength (φ = 0) separately. The φ = 0 factors are summarized in Table 5-7. An important difference is that the lumped correction factor is additive, yielding:

Ψc,BH,φ=0 = 1 + sc + dc + ic – bc – gc  (5-21)

where:
Ψc,BH,φ=0 = Brinch Hansen correction factor for Nc term for φ = 0 analysis.

The Brinch Hansen factors for unsaturated undrained (φ > 0) and drained conditions are summarized in Table 5-8. Brinch Hansen did not provide factors for the Nc term. Three options are available to address this shortcoming:
• Use Brinch Hansen's alternative bearing capacity equation, which is provided in the notes to Table 5-8,
• Ignore the contribution of the Nc term, which is often an appropriately conservative assumption, or
• Use the c factors provided in Table 5-8, which are based on the relationship between Nc and Nq (Hansen 1961, de Beer 1970).

For vertical loading, the bearing capacity of a rectangular foundation is controlled by the narrower dimension (B). However, load inclination may cause the longer dimension to control. The direction of the horizontal loading should be considered when calculating the inclination factors in Table 5-7 and Table 5-8.
key_points: Brinch Hansen (1970) handles the most complicating factors: shape, depth, load inclination, base inclination, and ground inclination.
For φ = 0, the lumped Nc correction factor is ADDITIVE: Ψc,BH,φ=0 = 1 + sc + dc + ic – bc – gc (Eq. 5-21), unlike the multiplicative form for other methods.

For φ > 0 and drained conditions, Brinch Hansen did not provide Nc term factors; three workarounds exist: use alternative equation, ignore Nc, or use derived c factors from Hansen (1961)/de Beer (1970).
Shape factors are adjusted (reduced) under inclined loading, similar to Meyerhof.
For rectangular foundations, load inclination direction determines whether the short or long dimension controls bearing capacity.
φ = 0 factors and φ > 0/drained factors are tabulated separately in Table 5-7 and Table 5-8 respectively.

equations.description: Brinch Hansen additive lumped correction factor for Nc term under φ = 0 conditions: Ψc,BH,φ=0 = 1 + sc + dc + ic – bc – gc

sections.applicability: Applies when using the Brinch Hansen (1970) bearing capacity method, particularly when multiple complicating factors (shape, depth, inclination, base slope, ground slope) must be considered simultaneously.

sections.title: Foundations Near the Top of Slopes
sections.summary: Covers bearing capacity analysis for foundations placed near slopes, which can reduce soil bearing capacity. Introduces two solution methods (Leshchinsky & Xie 2017; Meyerhof 1957) using a reduction coefficient (RCslope) approach for strip foundations. Discusses geometry, applicability, and cautions on depth factors and embedment effects when a slope is present.
sections.body:
In some cases, foundations must be placed near slopes, which may reduce the bearing capacity of the soil. Many procedures have been proposed with varying levels of complexity. The solutions by Leshchinsky and Xie (2017) and Meyerhof (1957) have been selected for their relative simplicity and general applicability using the geometry summarized in Figure 5-8. These solutions are for strip foundations and can be used as a conservative estimate for rectangular foundations. The shape factors from Section 5-3.3 may be appropriate but have not been fully explored by numerical or laboratory testing.

Saturated undrained conditions and drained conditions are considered separately in this section. The Leshchinsky and Xie (2017) approach ignores the effects of embedment, which is an appropriately conservative assumption if the foundation is relatively close to the slope. The depth factors in Table 5-6 to Table 5-8 do not include slope effects and should not be included. A comprehensive method that incorporates embedment depth can be found in Yang et al. (2019). The Yang et al. method can accommodate any combination of shear strength parameters. Slope stability software can also model foundation loading and can be used to explore this condition in more detail.
key_points: Foundations near slopes may have reduced bearing capacity; Leshchinsky & Xie (2017) and Meyerhof (1957) methods are selected for simplicity and general applicability.
Solutions are derived for strip foundations; use as conservative estimate for rectangular foundations.
Leshchinsky & Xie (2017) ignores embedment effects — appropriately conservative for foundations close to slopes.
Depth factors from Table 5-6 to 5-8 do NOT account for slope effects and must not be applied when a slope is present.
Yang et al. (2019) provides a comprehensive method incorporating embedment depth and any combination of shear strength parameters.
Slope stability software can be used for more detailed analysis of foundation loading near slopes.
figures: Figure 5-8
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating bearing capacity of foundations placed near the top of slopes where slope geometry may reduce soil bearing capacity.

sections.title: Saturated Undrained Conditions
sections.summary: Provides the method for computing bearing capacity reduction for foundations near slopes under saturated undrained conditions (su, φ=0). Defines the stability number NS = γH/su and uses RCslope from Table 5-9 (Leshchinsky & Xie 2017) based on B/H, b/B, slope angle β, and NS. Slope effects are small unless b/B < 2.5 or β > 30°.
sections.body:
For saturated undrained conditions (su, φ = 0), the effect of the slope tends to be small unless the foundation is close to the slope (b/B < 2.5) or the slope is steep (β > 30°). The influence of the stability of the slope on bearing capacity can be incorporated using a stability number defined as:

NS = γ·H / su  (5-22)

where:
γ = total unit weight of the soil,
H = slope height, and
su = undrained shear strength of the soil.

The ultimate bearing capacity for foundations near slopes is calculated using a reduction coefficient (RCslope) as indicated in Figure 5-8. Table 5-9 provides values of RCslope based on foundation dimensions (B/H), distance from the slope (b/B), slope angle (β), and slope stability number (NS) (Leshchinsky and Xie 2017). Interpolation should be used to determine RCslope for intermediate conditions. For steeper slopes or larger b/B, Leshchinsky and Xie (2017) should be consulted.
key_points: Slope effects on undrained bearing capacity are small unless b/B < 2.5 or β > 30°.
Stability number NS = γH/su captures the influence of slope stability on bearing capacity (Eq. 5-22).
RCslope from Table 5-9 depends on B/H, b/B, slope angle β, and stability number NS.
Interpolation is required for intermediate conditions not tabulated in Table 5-9.
Leshchinsky and Xie (2017) should be consulted directly for steeper slopes or larger b/B ratios.

equations.description: Stability number for undrained conditions: NS = γ·H / su, where γ is total unit weight, H is slope height, and su is undrained shear strength.

figures: Figure 5-8
sections.applicability: Applies when computing bearing capacity reduction for foundations near slopes under saturated undrained (φ=0) conditions.

sections.title: Drained Conditions
sections.summary: Addresses bearing capacity reduction for foundations near slopes under drained conditions, where slope effects are more significant than undrained. Uses RCslope from Table 5-10 (Leshchinsky & Xie 2017) with a stability number NS = γH/c′. For c′=0 conditions, Meyerhof (1957) chart method with Nγ,slope factors from Figure 5-9 is used instead. Largest reductions occur at low b/B and steep slopes.
sections.body:
For drained conditions, the effect of the slope on bearing capacity can be more significant. The reduction in bearing capacity depends on the effective stress friction angle in addition to similar factors as the undrained case. Table 5-10 summarizes reduction coefficients for common conditions encountered in engineering practice where cʹ > 0. Coefficients for B/H = 2 and other slope angles are available in Leshchinsky and Xie (2017). For conditions with cʹ = 0, the Meyerhof (1957) method presented at the end of this section can be used.

For soils modeled using an effective stress cohesion intercept, a stability number is required to incorporate its influence as:

NS = γ·H / cʹ  (5-23)

where:
γ = unit weight of the soil considering groundwater effects (Section 5-3.2),
H = slope height, and
cʹ = effective cohesion intercept of the soil.

As indicated in Figure 5-8, the reduced bearing capacity is found by multiplying RCslope with qult for non-sloping conditions with no embedment. The largest reductions in bearing capacity occur for foundations with low b/B ratios and steep slopes.

The reduction coefficients provided in Table 5-10 are for NS less than 2, which indicates relatively high values of cʹ. Leshchinsky and Xie also provide coefficients for Ns = 4. For these higher stability numbers, the stability of the slope itself is likely controlling, or the situation is dominated by frictional strength and it may be appropriate to ignore the effects of cʹ.

When cʹ is absent or ignored, the chart solution provided by Meyerhof (1957) can be used and is provided in Figure 5-9. Meyerhof provided factors (Nγ,slope) for embedment effects for Df/B = 1 and recommended interpolation for intermediate embedment ratios. As indicated in Figure 5-8, the Nq term is not used to calculate bearing capacity because its contribution is included in the values of Nγ,slope.
key_points: Slope effects on drained bearing capacity are more significant than undrained and also depend on effective friction angle φ′.
Stability number NS = γH/c′ (Eq. 5-23) incorporates the influence of effective cohesion on slope-affected bearing capacity.
RCslope from Table 5-10 is applied by multiplying with qult for flat-ground, no-embedment conditions.
Table 5-10 covers NS ≤ 2; for NS = 4 or higher, slope stability may govern or c′ effects can be ignored.
For c′ = 0 conditions, Meyerhof (1957) chart method (Figure 5-9) using Nγ,slope factors is used; the Nq term is excluded.
Meyerhof (1957) provides Nγ,slope for Df/B = 1 with interpolation recommended for intermediate embedment ratios.
Largest bearing capacity reductions occur for low b/B ratios and steep slopes.

equations.description: Stability number for drained conditions: NS = γ·H / c′, where γ is unit weight considering groundwater, H is slope height, and c′ is effective cohesion intercept.

figures: Figure 5-8
Figure 5-9
sections.applicability: Applies when computing bearing capacity reduction for foundations near slopes under drained conditions, with or without effective cohesion intercept c′.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Examples
sections.summary: Provides detailed worked examples demonstrating the application of the Terzaghi, Meyerhof, and Brinch Hansen bearing capacity methods. Illustrates use of shape, depth, and inclination factors. Eccentricity calculations using both the Meyerhof and Brinch Hansen approaches are also included. Examples are presented graphically in Figures 5-10 through 5-13.
sections.body: Figure 5-10 to Figure 5-12 provide detailed examples of the application of the Terzaghi, Meyerhof, and Brinch Hansen methods for bearing capacity analysis. They illustrate the use of shape, depth, and inclination factors. Eccentricity calculations using both the Meyerhof and Brinch Hansen approaches are provided in Figure 5-13.
key_points: Worked examples are provided for three bearing capacity methods: Terzaghi, Meyerhof, and Brinch Hansen.
Figure 5-10 illustrates the Terzaghi method with the Meyerhof method used as a check.
Figure 5-11 illustrates example calculations using the Meyerhof method.
Figure 5-12 illustrates example calculations using the Brinch Hansen method.
Figure 5-13 covers eccentricity calculations for both the Meyerhof and Brinch Hansen approaches.
Examples demonstrate practical application of shape, depth, and inclination correction factors.
figures: Figure 5-10 Example Calculations Illustrating the Terzaghi Method with the Meyerhof Method Used as a Check
Figure 5-11 Example Calculations Illustrating the Meyerhof Method
Figure 5-12 Example Calculations Illustrating the Brinch Hansen Method
Figure 5-13 Eccentricity Calculations – Meyerhof and Brinch Hansen Methods
sections.applicability: Applies when performing bearing capacity analyses using the Terzaghi, Meyerhof, or Brinch Hansen methods and needing worked examples that include shape, depth, inclination, and eccentricity factors.

sections.title: Nonuniform Soil and Layered Stratigraphy
sections.summary: Introduces four cases for bearing capacity analysis in non-uniform and layered soil conditions: (1) undrained clay with increasing su with depth, (2) undrained layered clay, (3) mixed unsaturated soils (c-φ), and (4) sand over clay. Layering must be considered when the top of the lower layer is within the depth of general shear failure (conservatively taken as B below bearing elevation).
sections.body:
Soil conditions are rarely uniform as assumed by the bearing capacity theories. For example, clays are often modeled using an undrained shear strength that increases with depth. Layered soils may present a problem for bearing capacity analysis when the strength of the two layers differs significantly. Layering must be considered when the top of the lower layer is above the maximum depth of general shear failure. In this case, both layers contribute to the bearing capacity of the footing. Zone II (Figure 5-4) typically extends to a depth of about 0.85B to B below the bearing elevation. Conservatively, this depth has been assumed to equal B for these methods. Four cases can be considered for layered soils as follows:
• Case 1: Undrained – increasing su with depth,
• Case 2: Undrained – layered clay,
• Case 3: Undrained – mixed unsaturated soils (c-φ), and
• Case 4: Sand (drained, cʹ = 0) over clay (undrained, su).
Figure 5-14 illustrates the conditions used for these four cases. Each of these cases is discussed in the following paragraphs.
key_points: Layering must be considered when the top of the lower layer is above the maximum depth of general shear failure (~B below bearing elevation).
Zone II extends approximately 0.85B to B below bearing elevation; B is conservatively used for all four case methods.
Four distinct cases cover the primary layered/non-uniform soil scenarios encountered in practice.
Both layers contribute to bearing capacity when the lower layer top is within the failure zone.
figures: Figure 5-14 Non-uniform and Stratified Soils Conditions – (a) Case 1 and (b) Cases 2 to 4
sections.applicability: Applies when soil conditions are non-uniform or layered and the lower layer top falls within the depth of general shear failure below the footing.

sections.title: Case 1: Undrained Clay - Increasing su with Depth
sections.summary: Covers bearing capacity for undrained clay where shear strength increases linearly with depth, typical of normally and some overconsolidated clays. Uses the Chi and Lin (2020) upper-bound plasticity solution for Nc for a smooth strip footing, expressed as a function of the surface cohesion su0 and rate of increase k. Solutions are plotted in Figure 5-15 and an example in Figure 5-16.
sections.body:
Case 1 represents typical strength gain with depth for normally and some overconsolidated clays, as illustrated in Figure 5-14(a). The bearing capacity will increase as a result of increased strength with depth. Davis and Booker (1973) considered this in terms of the undrained strength ratio.

Based on an upper bound plasticity solution, Chi and Lin (2020) suggested that the bearing capacity factor, Nc, for a perfectly smooth strip footing on clay soil with increasing strength with depth can be found as:

Nc = 5.14 + (k·B / su0)

where:
su0 = cohesion at surface of clay layer,
B = footing width, and
k = rate of increase in su with depth.

Solutions for Nc from Davis and Booker (1973) and Chi and Lin (2020) are plotted in Figure 5-15. Equation 5-22 lies between the solutions for perfectly smooth and perfectly rough footings. Since footings are neither perfectly smooth nor perfectly rough, this approach is a good fit for actual footings. Bearing capacity is determined using the calculated value of Nc and su0. An example is provided in Figure 5-16.
key_points: Applies to normally and lightly overconsolidated clays where su increases linearly with depth.
Nc = 5.14 + (k·B / su0) per Chi and Lin (2020) upper-bound plasticity solution for a smooth strip footing.
The equation lies between smooth and rough footing solutions, making it appropriate for real footings.
Bearing capacity is computed using the calculated Nc multiplied by the surface cohesion su0.
Figure 5-15 provides graphical comparison of Nc solutions from Davis & Booker (1973) and Chi & Lin (2020).

equations.description: Bearing capacity factor Nc for smooth strip footing on undrained clay with linearly increasing strength with depth: Nc = 5.14 + (k·B / su0), where su0 is surface cohesion, B is footing width, and k is rate of increase of su with depth.

figures: Figure 5-15 Variation of Nc for Clay with Increasing su with Depth (after Chi and Lin 2020)
Figure 5-16 Bearing Capacity Example – Increasing Strength with Depth (Case 1)
sections.applicability: Applies when bearing capacity analysis involves undrained clay with shear strength increasing linearly with depth below the footing.

sections.title: Case 2: Undrained, Layered Clay
sections.summary: Addresses bearing capacity for two-layer undrained clay profiles using modified bearing capacity factors (Nc,m,s and Nc,m,c) from Brown and Meyerhof (1969). Covers both soft-over-stiff (squeezing failure) and stiff-over-soft (punching failure) cases. Provides Eq. 5-25 to interpolate rectangular foundation factor Nc,m,r from strip and circular values. Inclination factors should not be combined with these modified factors.
sections.body:
Layered clay stratigraphy occurs often in practice. For example, a younger post-glacial low strength clay may overlay an older stiffer clay. In other cases, a stiffer clay, created by desiccation, may overlay a softer clay.

When the top layer is softer or weaker than the underlying clay, the failure occurs in the upper soft layer or along the interface of the two layers. A squeezing type failure occurs above or along the boundary rather than a classic general shear failure. Brown and Meyerhof (1969) presented the relationships shown in Figure 5-18 to estimate modified bearing capacity factors (Nc,m,s and Nc,m,c) for strip and circular footings on two layer clay systems. The right side of the figure is used for conditions where the upper layer is soft. When the top of the strong layer is more than 70% of the foundation width below the bearing elevation (H / B ≥ 0.7), the bearing capacity is not affected by the presence of the stronger layer. Table 5-11 presents ranges of modified bearing capacity factors for these conditions.

When the stiffer or stronger layer is on top, the footing tends to punch through the stiff layer into the soft layer developing a general shear failure in the soft clay as shown in Figure 5-17(b). The equations provided in Figure 5-18 can be used when the top layer is stiffer or stronger. The undrained strength of the top layer is used to calculate bearing capacity with these modified bearing capacity factors. When 0.7 < su2/su1 < 1, it is prudent to reduce the values of Nc,m,s and Nc,m,c by 10 percent. When the weak layer is more than three foundation widths below the bearing elevation (H / B > 3), the bearing capacity is not affected by the presence of the deeper layer.

For a layered clay soil profile, the modified bearing capacity for a rectangular foundation (Nc,m,r) can be estimated from the circular and strip factors as:

Nc,m,r = Nc,m,c · (B/L) + Nc,m,s · (1 - B/L)

where:
Nc,m,s = modified bearing capacity factor for strip footing - Figure 5-18(a),
Nc,m,c = modified bearing capacity factor for circular footing - Figure 5-18(b),
B = rectangular foundation width, and
L = rectangular foundation length.

The effect of overburden (Nq = 1) may be included along with the Nc,m factors discussed in this section. Inclination factors should not be combined with these modified bearing capacity factors. An example is provided in Figure 5-19.
key_points: Soft-over-stiff clay produces a squeezing failure; strong layer has no effect when H/B ≥ 0.7 (soft on top).
Stiff-over-soft clay produces a punching failure into the soft layer; weak layer has no effect when H/B > 3.
Reduce Nc,m,s and Nc,m,c by 10% when 0.7 < su2/su1 < 1 (nearly uniform strength ratio).
Nc,m,r for rectangular footings is interpolated between strip (Nc,m,s) and circular (Nc,m,c) factors using B/L ratio (Eq. 5-25).
Inclination factors must NOT be combined with the modified bearing capacity factors from Brown and Meyerhof (1969).
Overburden effect (Nq = 1) may be added to the Nc,m-based bearing capacity.

equations.description: Modified bearing capacity factor for rectangular footing on layered clay: Nc,m,r = Nc,m,c·(B/L) + Nc,m,s·(1 - B/L), interpolating between circular (Nc,m,c) and strip (Nc,m,s) factors by B/L ratio.

Figure 5-18 Modified Bearing Capacity Factors for Two-Layer Clay Stratigraphy for a) Strip and b) Circular Footings (after Brown and Meyerhof 1969)
Figure 5-19 Bearing Capacity Example – Layered, Undrained Clay (Case 2)

sections.applicability: Applies when bearing capacity analysis involves two-layer undrained clay profiles where layer strengths differ significantly and the lower layer top is within depth B of the bearing elevation.

sections.title: Case 3: Mixed Soil Layers - Unsaturated Undrained
sections.summary: Provides the Satyanarayana and Garg (1980) method for bearing capacity of mixed sand-and-clay profiles under unsaturated, undrained (c-φ) conditions. Defines equations for the effective thickness of the second layer (Eq. 5-26) and weighted-average shear strength parameters cave and φave (Eqs. 5-27, 5-28) to use with Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory.
sections.body:
The bearing capacity of mixed soil profiles of sand and clay can be evaluated using the method by Satyanarayana and Garg (1980). The method was validated using unsaturated, compacted samples and should be considered applicable to unsaturated, undrained conditions characterized by c-φ parameters. Unless a rigid boundary is encountered as shown in Figure 5-14(b), the thickness of the second layer is defined as:

H2 = (B/2·tan φ1 + c1) / (tan φ2 + c2/H1) - H1

where:
B = width of strip footing,
H1 = thickness of top layer below bearing elevation,
c1, c2 = undrained cohesion of top and bottom layers, respectively, and
φ1, φ2 = undrained friction angle of top and bottom layers, respectively.

The average shear strength parameters calculated as:

cave = (H1·c1 + H2·c2) / (H1 + H2)

and

φave = arctan((H1·tan φ1 + H2·tan φ2) / (H1 + H2))

These parameters should be used with Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory.
key_points: Applicable to unsaturated, undrained mixed sand-clay profiles characterized by c-φ parameters (Satyanarayana and Garg 1980).
Eq. 5-26 defines the effective second-layer thickness H2, unless a rigid boundary limits it.
Average cohesion cave (Eq. 5-27) is a thickness-weighted linear average of the two layers.
Average friction angle φave (Eq. 5-28) is computed from a thickness-weighted average of tan φ values.
Averaged c and φ parameters are used directly with Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory.

equations.description: Effective thickness of second layer H2 for mixed unsaturated soil profile: H2 = [(B/2)·tan φ1 + c1] / [tan φ2 + c2/H1] - H1, where B is strip footing width, H1 is top layer thickness, c and φ are cohesion and friction angle of respective layers.
Weighted-average undrained cohesion for mixed soil layers: cave = (H1·c1 + H2·c2) / (H1 + H2).
Weighted-average undrained friction angle for mixed soil layers: φave = arctan[(H1·tan φ1 + H2·tan φ2) / (H1 + H2)].

figures: Figure 5-20 Bearing Capacity Example – Mixed Soil Layers (Case 3)
sections.applicability: Applies when bearing capacity analysis involves mixed unsaturated undrained soil profiles (sand and clay) characterized by c-φ parameters, with two distinct layers beneath the footing.

sections.title: Case 4: Sand Layer Over Clay
sections.summary: Covers Meyerhof (1974) method for shallow foundations on sand overlying clay. Two failure modes are possible: punching through thin/dense sand into clay (passive force PP resists load) or failure confined within thick/loose sand. Coefficients Ks and s·Ks (Figure 5-22) govern punching resistance. For sand over stiff clay or rock, modified bearing capacity/shape factors (Figure 5-24) are used with Eq. 5-15; compared against underlying clay capacity.
sections.body:
Meyerhof (1974) investigated shallow foundations on layers of sand and clay. In some cases, surficial layers of sand or coarse-grained soil are underlain by clay. The sand layer may be natural or a layer of engineered fill. Figure 5-21 shows two possibilities. A thin and/or dense layer of sand is depicted on the left, and the bearing capacity failure surface may break through the sand into the clay. A passive force (PP) develops along the failure surface through the sand, which helps to resist the foundation loading.

When the sand is loose or thick, the bearing capacity failure surface may remain within the sand layer as shown in Figure 5-21(b). The location of the failure depends on the relative density of the sand, the ratio of the footing width to the depth of the sand below the bearing elevation, H1, and the relative strength of the underlying clay. If both strata have similar individual bearing capacities, the bearing capacity failure surface may extend into the clay.

The coefficients, Ks and s·Ks, can be estimated using the trends in Figure 5-22. The value of δ/φʹ is for the inclination of the passive force on the failure surface through the sand as shown in Figure 5-21. Model tests by Meyerhof (1974) and field observations of full-sized footings indicate that the theoretical trends can be safely used. Meyerhof and Hanna (1978) show that δ/φʹ increases to 1 as the bearing capacity of the clay approaches the bearing capacity of the sand. An example is provided in Figure 5-23.

If stiff clay or rock lies below the sand, the thin sand layer may squeeze out from under the footing as it fails. The bearing capacity and shape factors applicable to this situation depend on the ratio of H1 / B, where H1 is the thickness of the sand layer below the bearing elevation. The modified bearing capacity and shape factors can be found in Figure 5-24 and should be used with Equation 5-15. The bearing capacity calculated using the modified factors should be compared to the bearing capacity of the underlying stiff clay. If the bearing capacity of the clay is lower, it should be used instead.
key_points: Two failure modes: punching through thin/dense sand into clay (with passive resistance PP), or failure contained within loose/thick sand.
Failure mode depends on sand relative density, H1/B ratio, and relative strength of sand vs. clay layers.
Ks and s·Ks coefficients (Figure 5-22) quantify punching shear resistance; δ/φʹ approaches 1 as clay strength approaches sand strength.
For sand over stiff clay/rock, sand may squeeze laterally; use modified factors from Figure 5-24 with Eq. 5-15.
Always compare calculated bearing capacity to that of the underlying clay; use the lower value.

equations.description: Referenced bearing capacity equation to be used with modified bearing capacity and shape factors from Figure 5-24 for the case of sand over stiff clay or rock.

figures: Figure 5-21 Bearing Capacity of Sand Over Relatively Weak Clay (after Meyerhof 1974)
Figure 5-22 Coefficients Ks and s·Ks for Punching Shearing Resistance (after Meyerhof 1974, Meyerhof and Hanna 1978)
Figure 5-23 Bearing Capacity Example – Sand Layer Over Clay (Case 4)
Figure 5-24 Modified bearing capacity and shape factors for sand over stiff clay or rock
sections.applicability: Applies when a shallow foundation is founded on a sand or coarse-grained layer (natural or engineered fill) overlying a clay or rock stratum.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity of Rock
sections.summary: Covers the calculation of bearing capacity for rock foundations using the Terzaghi method with rock-specific bearing capacity factors based on the rock fracture friction angle (including asperity effects). Addresses three shear strength parameter types for rock, typical φ' values for rock fractures and joints, and RQD-based reduction of ultimate bearing capacity. Recommends a factor of safety of 3–4 for rock foundations.
sections.body:
Three types of shear strength parameters are used in rock mechanics depending on the rock structure being evaluated: 1) shearing of an intact specimen, 2) shearing along a joint or fracture, or 3) shearing through a fractured rock mass. For bearing capacity, shearing along a rock fracture is the most applicable.

Table 5-12 provides typical φʹ values for rock fractures and joints. Rock fractures have undulations or irregularities called asperities, which add to the frictional resistance of smooth rock fractures (Stagg and Zienkiewicz 1968). The asperity angle (i) usually ranges from 10 to 15°. The design friction angle (φʹrf) is found by adding the rock friction angle, such as those in Table 5-12, and the asperity angle.

The bearing capacity of rock may be calculated using the Terzaghi method along with the Terzaghi shape factors (Table 5-5). However, the bearing capacity factors are different for rock and are given by Stagg and Zienkiewicz (1968) based on φʹrf as given in Equations 5-29, 5-30, and 5-31.

The evaluation of rock bearing capacity should also include some measure of the rock quality, such as Rock Quality Designation (RQD) or Geological Strength Index (GSI). RQD can be incorporated as a reduction to the ultimate bearing capacity as suggested by Bowles (1996) in Equation 5-32, where qʹult = reduced ultimate bearing capacity.

For Equation 5-32, the RQD should be evaluated to a depth of B below the footing and should be expressed as a decimal, not a percentage. A factor of safety of 3 to 4 is recommended to calculate qall,net from qʹult for rock foundations. When using RQD, the rock material must meet the hardness and soundness criteria defined by Deere and Deere (1989). In massive rock with few fractures, the RQD will likely be 100 percent (1.0), and the qʹult value will equal qult.
key_points: For bearing capacity of rock, shearing along a rock fracture (joint) is the most applicable failure mode of the three shear strength types used in rock mechanics.
The design rock fracture friction angle (φʹrf) equals the base rock friction angle (from Table 5-12) plus the asperity angle, which typically ranges from 10 to 15°.
Rock bearing capacity factors Nc, Nq, and Nγ differ from soil values and are functions of φʹrf per Stagg and Zienkiewicz (1968); Terzaghi shape factors (Table 5-5) are still applicable.
RQD reduces ultimate bearing capacity by the factor RQD²; RQD must be evaluated as a decimal over a depth of B below the footing.
A factor of safety of 3 to 4 is recommended when calculating qall,net from the RQD-reduced ultimate bearing capacity qʹult for rock foundations.
In massive rock with few fractures (RQD ≈ 1.0), qʹult equals qult with no reduction.
Rock quality measures such as RQD or GSI should supplement bearing capacity calculations; rock must meet Deere and Deere (1989) hardness and soundness criteria when using RQD.

equations.description: Rock bearing capacity factor Nc as a function of rock fracture friction angle: Nc = 5·tan⁴(45 + φʹrf/2)
Rock bearing capacity factor Nq as a function of rock fracture friction angle: Nq = tan⁶(45 + φʹrf/2)
Rock bearing capacity factor Nγ defined in terms of Nq: Nγ = Nq + 1
RQD-reduced ultimate bearing capacity for rock: qʹult = qult · RQD², where RQD is expressed as a decimal evaluated to depth B below the footing

figures: Figure 5-24
sections.applicability: Applies when calculating the bearing capacity of rock foundations, including consideration of fracture friction angle, asperity effects, and rock quality via RQD.

sections.title: Definitions and Applications
sections.summary: Introduces combined, continuous, grid, mat, rigid, and flexible foundation types for shallow foundations carrying more than a single column or wall load. Clarifies when each type is appropriate, emphasizes the iterative design process between geotechnical and structural engineers for mat foundations, and notes that slabs-on-grade are excluded.
sections.body:
This section considers the design of shallow foundations carrying more than a single column or wall load as defined above. The following definitions are helpful and have been summarized from ACI (2002):
• Combined footing – footing supporting more than one column load. Combined footings are used when column loads are closely spaced so that individual footings would overlap and thus the footings are combined to support the loads.
• Continuous footing – footing supporting two or more columns in a row. Continuous foundations are used under wall loads and when the distance between columns is sufficiently close that individual footings can be combined.
• Grid foundation – a foundation formed by intersecting continuous footings. Grid foundations are a variation on continuous footings.
• Mat foundation – a continuous footing supporting columns in several rows in each direction, covering an area of at least 75 percent of the total structure area. Mat foundations are generally appropriate if: 1) the sum of individual footing base areas exceeds about 75% of the total foundation area; 2) the subsurface strata contain cavities or compressible lenses and differential settlements are a concern; 3) the subsurface strata are highly compressible and a reduction in bearing pressures is helpful; or 4) resistance to hydrostatic uplift is required.
• Rigid foundation – loads cause differential to total settlement ratios ≤ 0.1.
• Flexible foundation – does not meet requirements for rigid foundations.
Design of these foundations, especially mats, is an iterative process between the geotechnical engineer and the structural engineer. The soil response is based on mat contact pressures, which in turn are based on mat loads, flexibility, and modulus. Thus, the computed mat deflections and soil responses must converge. Economic considerations will also have an impact on selection of a combined footing and mat foundation over other alternatives. Slabs-on-grade are excluded from this discussion.
key_points: Combined footing supports more than one column; used when individual footings would overlap.

Mat foundation covers ≥75% of total structure area; appropriate when individual footing areas exceed ~75% of total foundation area, differential settlement is a concern, strata are highly compressible, or uplift resistance is needed.
Rigid foundation: differential-to-total settlement ratio ≤ 0.1; flexible foundation does not meet this criterion.
Mat foundation design is iterative between geotechnical and structural engineers — contact pressures, flexibility, and modulus must converge.
Slabs-on-grade are explicitly excluded from this section's scope.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing shallow foundations that carry more than a single column or wall load, including combined, continuous, grid, and mat foundations.

sections.title: Definitions and Applications
sections.summary: Provides ACI (2002)-sourced definitions for combined, continuous, grid, mat, rigid, and flexible foundations, and describes when each type is appropriate. Highlights that mat foundation design is iterative between structural and geotechnical engineers, with soil response dependent on contact pressures, flexibility, and modulus convergence.
