The soil response is based on mat contact pressures, which in turn are based on mat loads, flexibility, and modulus. Thus, the computed mat deflections and soil responses must converge. Economic considerations will also have an impact on selection of a combined footing and mat foundation over other alternatives. Slabs-on-grade are excluded from this discussion.
key_points: Combined footing supports more than one column; used when individual footings would overlap.

Mat foundation covers ≥75% of total structure area; warranted when individual footing areas exceed ~75% of total foundation area, differential settlement risk is high, strata are highly compressible, or uplift resistance is needed.
Rigid foundation defined by differential-to-total settlement ratio ≤ 0.1.
Mat design requires iterative convergence between structural and geotechnical engineers on contact pressures, mat flexibility, and soil modulus.
Slabs-on-grade are explicitly excluded from this discussion.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and defining the appropriate type of multi-column or multi-wall shallow foundation (combined, continuous, grid, mat, rigid, or flexible).

sections.title: Rigid Foundations
sections.summary: Describes the behavior and design assumptions for rigid foundations, which prevent differential settlement between columns or walls due to their stiffness. Explains that contact pressures are non-uniform for ideal coarse-grained or saturated fine-grained soils (Figure 5-26), but that structural engineers acceptably assume average contact pressure per ACI (2002). Also covers linear non-uniform contact pressure for non-uniform loads.
sections.body: Rigid foundations are those which, because of their stiffness, will not allow individual columns or walls to settle differentially. Rigid foundations produce uniform settlements if loaded uniformly. The contact pressures, however, are not uniform for ideal coarse-grained soil (cʹ = 0 psf) or saturated fine-grained soil (φ = 0), as shown in Figure 5-26. In design, structural engineers generally assume the contact pressure to be an average of the total load on the foundation divided by the area of the foundation for these rigid foundations. This is an acceptable approach according to ACI (2002) because of conservative load estimates used for calculation of settlement and an ample safety factor against the ultimate bearing capacity. Many foundations, however, support loads that are not uniform. It is common practice, in these cases, to assume a linear, nonuniform contact pressure, such as under a retaining wall where the toe pressure is maximum and the heel pressure is minimum.
key_points: Rigid foundations prevent differential settlement between columns/walls due to structural stiffness.
Rigid foundations produce uniform settlements under uniform loading, but contact pressures are non-uniform for ideal coarse-grained (cʹ=0) or saturated fine-grained (φ=0) soils.
ACI (2002) accepts average contact pressure assumption (total load / foundation area) due to conservative load estimates and ample bearing capacity safety factors.
For non-uniform loads, linear non-uniform contact pressure is assumed (e.g., retaining walls: maximum at toe, minimum at heel).
See Figure 5-26 for idealized contact pressure and settlement distributions under rigid foundations.
figures: Figure 5-26 Idealized Distribution of Contact Pressure and Settlement Under a Uniformly Distributed Load for a Rigid Foundation - a) Coarse-grained (cʹ = 0 psf) and b) Fine-grained (φ = 0°) (after Das 2022)
sections.applicability: Applies when designing combined footings or mat foundations that are sufficiently stiff to be classified as rigid, and when determining appropriate contact pressure assumptions for structural design.

sections.title: Rigid Foundation Criteria
sections.summary: Presents Meyerhof's (1953) relative stiffness factor Kr (Eq. 5-33) to determine whether combined footings or mat foundations qualify as rigid. When Kr ≥ 0.5, the differential-to-total settlement ratio is ≤ 0.1 and the foundation is considered rigid. Describes the collaborative role of structural and geotechnical engineers in computing Kr, including use of the factor λ for continuous foundations.
sections.body:
Combined footings and mat foundations may be designed as rigid structures if they meet the relative stiffness factor criteria, Kr, developed by Meyerhof (1953):

Kr = (E′·Ib) / (Es · B³)

where:
E′·Ib = flexural stiffness of the structure (beyond scope of this document),
Es = soil modulus, and
B = width of foundation.

Calculation of the relative stiffness is a joint effort of the structural and geotechnical engineers. A preliminary Es value must be provided by the geotechnical engineer to the structural engineer. An approximate value of stiffness per unit width of building and foundation width is estimated by the structural engineer. Using this information, the structural engineer calculates the relative stiffness, Kr, of a foundation. The structural engineer should indicate to the geotechnical engineer whether the foundation is rigid or flexible, or whether both types of foundations should be considered by the geotechnical engineer. When Kr ≥ 0.5, the ratio of differential to total settlement is about 0.1 or less and the foundation may be considered rigid.

The spacing of columns can be used to determine if continuous foundations may be considered rigid using a factor (λ) based on soil and foundation stiffness.
key_points: Rigid foundation criterion: Kr ≥ 0.5, corresponding to differential-to-total settlement ratio ≤ 0.1 (Meyerhof 1953).
Kr = (E′·Ib) / (Es · B³), where E′·Ib is flexural stiffness, Es is soil modulus, and B is foundation width.
Geotechnical engineer provides preliminary Es; structural engineer estimates stiffness per unit width and computes Kr.
Structural engineer must communicate to geotechnical engineer whether foundation is rigid, flexible, or both conditions need consideration.
Column spacing can also be used to assess rigidity of continuous foundations via a stiffness-based factor λ.

equations.description: Relative stiffness factor Kr for combined footings and mat foundations: Kr = (E′·Ib) / (Es · B³), where E′·Ib is the flexural stiffness of the structure, Es is the soil modulus, and B is the foundation width. Kr ≥ 0.5 indicates a rigid foundation.

sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating whether a combined footing or mat foundation qualifies as rigid using Meyerhof's relative stiffness factor criterion.

sections.title: Flexible Foundation Criteria
sections.summary: Defines the criteria for classifying a foundation as flexible (Kr < 0.5) and describes design implications. Covers the relative flexibility parameter λ (Eq. 5-34), the rigid foundation threshold based on column spacing, and how flexible foundations are designed as beams on elastic foundations, including idealized contact pressure distributions for coarse- and fine-grained soils.
sections.body:
If Kr < 0.5, the foundation should be designed as a flexible foundation. For example, when Kr = 0, the ratio of differential settlement to total settlement is about 0.5 and 0.35 for continuous and square footings, respectively, according to ACI (2002).

If a foundation is considered flexible, it is usually designed by the structural engineer as a beam on elastic foundation. Figure 5-27 illustrates the contact pressure for these foundations when uniformly loaded and supported on ideal coarse-grained soil (c′ = 0) and fine-grained soil (φ = 0). The contact pressure will be uniform for a uniform load, and the settlement will be greatest at the edges of the foundation for coarse-grained soil and dish shaped (concave up) for a saturated clay with the greatest settlement at the center of the foundation.

The relative flexibility parameter λ is defined as:

λ = (ks · B · I)^(1/4) / (Ec · I)^(1/4)

where:
  ks = modulus of subgrade reaction (see Section 5-4.5),
  Ec = modulus of concrete, and
  I = moment of inertia of footing.

A foundation can be considered rigid if the average spacing of two adjacent column spans is less than 1.75/λ, provided adjacent column loads and column spacing do not vary by more than 20 percent. This assessment is typically completed by the structural engineer.

If the foundation meets either of these criteria, it may be designed as a rigid foundation with a linear distribution of soil pressure based on statics. Thus, the assumption for design is that a straight-line relationship exists between maximum and minimum contact pressures below the footing. In this case, the geotechnical engineer is responsible for providing a net allowable soil bearing pressure, qall,net, as described in Section 5-2.4. The settlement should be estimated using the methods of Chapter 5 of DM 7.1.
key_points: Foundation is classified as flexible when Kr < 0.5; at Kr = 0, differential-to-total settlement ratio is ~0.5 (continuous) or ~0.35 (square footing).
Flexible foundations are typically designed by the structural engineer as beams on an elastic foundation.
The relative flexibility parameter λ (Eq. 5-34) uses modulus of subgrade reaction (ks), modulus of concrete (Ec), footing width (B), and moment of inertia (I).
A foundation may be treated as rigid if average adjacent column spacing is less than 1.75/λ, provided loads and spacing vary ≤20%.
For coarse-grained soil (c′=0), settlement is greatest at foundation edges; for fine-grained saturated clay (φ=0), settlement is dish-shaped and greatest at center.
Geotechnical engineer provides net allowable soil bearing pressure qall,net (Section 5-2.4) when rigid foundation design is used; settlement estimated per DM 7.1 Chapter 5.

equations.description: Relative flexibility parameter λ for evaluating rigid vs. flexible foundation behavior: λ = (ks · B · I)^(1/4) / (Ec · I)^(1/4), where ks is the modulus of subgrade reaction, B is the footing width, Ec is the modulus of concrete, and I is the moment of inertia of the footing.

figures: Figure 5-27 Idealized Distribution of Contact Pressure and Settlement Under a Uniformly Distributed Loading for a Flexible Foundation – a) Fine-grained Soil (φ = 0 deg) and b) Coarse-grained Soil (c′ = 0) (after Das 2022)
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating whether a mat or combined footing should be designed as a flexible foundation (Kr < 0.5) and when determining appropriate contact pressure and settlement distributions for coarse- or fine-grained soils.

sections.title: Required Input for Analysis of Continuous and Mat Foundations
sections.summary: Describes the geotechnical input parameters required by structural engineers when designing continuous and mat foundations using FEM or FGM approaches. Covers soil-structure interaction challenges, factors that reduce accuracy of flexible foundation analysis, and the specific soil parameters (qall,net, s, Es, ν, ks) the geotechnical engineer must provide.
sections.body:
Most structural engineers use software to design continuous and mat foundations. Closed form analytical solutions are available for specific problems (Hetenyi 1948) but not more complex situations. The two procedures often used to evaluate the soil response for continuous footings or mat foundations are the finite element method (FEM) using elastic constants and the finite grid method (FGM) using a Winkler foundation model with elastic springs. The springs can be either coupled or uncoupled. The properties of these springs are estimated using a subgrade modulus (ks), which is adjusted for footing size or tributary area of a node for a mat. Consideration is also given to the change of subgrade modulus with depth. Uncoupled springs are a simplifying assumption that structural engineers may use in their design.

Flexible foundations present significant soil structure interaction issues that require the geotechnical engineer and structural engineer to work together to find an appropriate solution. When the relative stiffness factor indicates the foundation may be borderline rigid/flexible, the structural engineer may choose to analyze the foundation as both a rigid and flexible structure. The analyses of a foundation as a flexible plate on an elastic foundation may appear to be a more exact approach. However, a number of factors reduce the accuracy of this approach, including:
• Difficulty in estimating and assigning elastic soil parameters: ks, Es, and ν,
• Horizontal and vertical variation of soil strata thickness and properties,
• Mat shape,
• Variety of superstructure loads and assumptions in their development, and
• Interaction effects between the superstructure stiffness and stiffness of the continuous footing or mat foundation.

Depending on whether an FEM or FGM approach is being used, the structural engineer may require the following input from geotechnical engineers for flexible foundation design:
• Net allowable soil bearing pressure, qall,net,
• Estimated settlement, s,
• Estimated soil modulus, Es,
• Poisson's ratio, ν, and
• Estimated modulus of subgrade reaction, ks.

Generally, the soil is not homogeneous under a combined footing or mat foundation and the geotechnical engineer must develop soil behavior and properties that represent the stratigraphy, loading condition, and depth of stress penetration. Estimation of the allowable bearing pressure was discussed in Sections 5-2 and 5-3. Methods of calculating the estimated settlement are included in Chapter 5 of DM 7.1. Methods to estimate ks, Es, and ν are discussed in the following section.
key_points: FEM (using elastic constants) and FGM (using Winkler springs) are the two primary methods for evaluating soil response under continuous or mat foundations.
Spring stiffness in FGM is characterized by subgrade modulus (ks), adjusted for footing size or tributary node area, with depth variation also considered.
Flexible foundations require close collaboration between geotechnical and structural engineers due to significant soil-structure interaction complexity.

Key factors limiting accuracy of flexible plate-on-elastic-foundation analysis include difficulty estimating ks/Es/ν, soil variability, mat shape, load variability, and superstructure-foundation stiffness interaction.

Required geotechnical inputs for FEM/FGM design include: net allowable bearing pressure (qall,net), estimated settlement (s), soil modulus (Es), Poisson's ratio (ν), and modulus of subgrade reaction (ks).
Soil is generally not homogeneous beneath mat foundations; geotechnical engineers must develop representative properties accounting for stratigraphy, loading, and stress penetration depth.
sections.applicability: Applies when a structural engineer requires geotechnical input parameters to design continuous footings or mat foundations using FEM or FGM flexible foundation analysis methods.

sections.title: Modulus of Subgrade Reaction
sections.summary: Defines the modulus of subgrade reaction (ks) as the ratio of contact pressure to settlement (force/cubic length). Introduces Eq. 5-35, provides typical ks values by soil type in Table 5-13, and notes that two estimation procedures (plate load tests and elastic parameters) are discussed in subsections. Table values should not be used to compute an average ks due to the wide range.
sections.body:
The modulus of subgrade reaction (ks) is the ratio of the contact pressure divided by the corresponding deformation, or settlement, and has the units of force per cubic length. Other names include the coefficient of subgrade reaction or subgrade reaction. The modulus of subgrade reaction is depicted in Figure 5-28 and can be calculated as:

ks = q / s  (5-35)

where:
q = contact pressure acting perpendicular to the contact area and
s = soil settlement.

Typical ks values are provided in Table 5-13 that can be used as a guide for comparison to measured or calculated values. The table should not be used to calculate an average value of ks because of the breadth of the range of values. Two procedures for estimating ks are discussed below.
key_points: ks is the ratio of contact pressure (q) to settlement (s); units are force per cubic length (e.g., pci).
Eq. 5-35: ks = q/s defines the modulus of subgrade reaction.
Table 5-13 gives typical ks ranges by soil type (e.g., loose sand 20–60 pci, dense sand 250–500 pci) for comparison only, not for design averaging.
Two estimation procedures are available: plate load tests (5-4.5.1) and elastic parameters (5-4.5.2).
Time-dependent effects (heave/recompression after excavation, long-term consolidation of clays) must be considered in mat foundation analysis.

equations.description: Modulus of subgrade reaction: ks = q / s, where q is contact pressure and s is soil settlement.

figures: Figure 5-28 Subgrade Pressure versus Settlement Curve Defining ks (after Bowles 1996)
tables: Table 5-13 Typical Modulus of Subgrade Reaction Values (after Bowles 1996)
sections.applicability: Applies when defining or estimating the modulus of subgrade reaction for mat or combined footing foundation design.

sections.title: Estimating ks from Plate Load Tests
sections.summary: Describes use of a 1-ft wide square or circular plate load test to estimate ks, noting the nonlinear pressure-deflection relationship and use of a secant modulus at a specific settlement (e.g., 1 inch). Provides Eq. 5-36 to scale plate test results to footings ≤5 ft wide. Warns that plate load test results cannot be scaled to larger footings or mats due to soil variability with depth.
sections.body:
A plate load test may be used to estimate ks, which pushes a 1-foot wide square or circular plate into the ground. The pressure and deflection are measured as shown in Figure 5-28. The pressure-deflection relationship is typically nonlinear. The secant modulus through a specific settlement point, for example 1-inch of settlement and the origin, is usually used to define ks for a plate load test.

The plate load test is of limited value for foundations due to the size of the plate and scale effects. If the combined footing has a width less than or equal to 5 ft with uniform soil conditions within the depth of influence (2B for square footings or 4B for continuous footings), the ks value for design of the footing may be approximated from a plate load test as suggested by Sowers (1977):

ks = kp (Bp / B)^n  (5-36)

where:
kp = the modulus of subgrade reaction from the plate load test,
Bp = width of plate,
B = width of foundation, and
n = 0.5 to 0.7.

Plate load test results cannot be scaled for larger footings and mats because of the variation of soil properties within the depth of stress penetration.
key_points: Plate load test uses a 1-ft wide square or circular plate; ks is defined as the secant modulus at a chosen settlement (e.g., 1 inch).
Eq. 5-36 scales plate test ks to a footing using ks = kp(Bp/B)^n, where n = 0.5 to 0.7.
Scaling is only valid for footings ≤5 ft wide with uniform soil within the depth of influence.
Plate load test results CANNOT be scaled to larger footings or mats due to soil variability with depth of stress penetration.
Depth of influence is 2B for square footings and 4B for continuous footings.

equations.description: Scaling plate load test ks to a footing: ks = kp * (Bp / B)^n, where kp is plate test modulus, Bp is plate width, B is foundation width, and n = 0.5 to 0.7 (Sowers 1977).

figures: Figure 5-28 Subgrade Pressure versus Settlement Curve Defining ks (after Bowles 1996)
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating ks for combined footings ≤5 ft wide with uniform soil conditions, using plate load test data.

sections.title: Estimating ks from Elastic Parameters
sections.summary: Derives ks from elastic settlement theory using soil elastic modulus (Es), Poisson's ratio (ν), and influence factors µ0 and µ1 that account for embedment depth, foundation shape, and depth to firm layer. Eq. 5-37 expresses ks = Es / (B·µ0·µ1). Influence factors are obtained from Figure 5-29 (after Giroud 1972 and Burland 1970).
sections.body:
Assuming the soil acts as an elastic medium, settlement can be estimated based on the foundation size and bearing pressure as well as the soil properties, Es and ν. Influence factors (µ0 and µ1) are used to account for depth of embedment, foundation shape and depth to a firm layer. These factors are provided in Figure 5-29.

Using the definition of ks in Equation 5-32, the elastic settlement equation can be rewritten as:

ks = q / s = 1 / (B·µ0·µ1 / Es)  (5-37)

where:
B = width of foundation,
Es = elastic modulus of the soil within the zone of influence for the foundation,
µ0 = influence factor related to embedment of the load and ν, and
µ1 = influence factor related to problem geometry and ν.
key_points: ks is derived from elastic settlement theory: ks = Es / (B·µ0·µ1) per Eq. 5-37.
µ0 accounts for embedment depth and Poisson's ratio; µ1 accounts for foundation geometry (shape, depth to firm layer) and ν.
Influence factors µ0 and µ1 are read from Figure 5-29 for ν = 0.5, 0.3, and 0.25.
This approach requires reliable estimates of Es and ν for the soil within the zone of influence.
References Eq. 5-32 for the base definition of ks used to rewrite the elastic settlement equation.

equations.description: ks from elastic parameters: ks = q/s = Es / (B·µ0·µ1), where B is foundation width, Es is soil elastic modulus, µ0 is embedment/Poisson influence factor, and µ1 is geometry/Poisson influence factor.

figures: Figure 5-29 Elastic Influence Factors - (a) µ1 with ν = 0.5, (b) µ1 with ν = 0.3, and (c) µ0 with ν = 0.25 and 0.5 (after Giroud 1972 and Burland 1970)
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating ks for mat or combined footing foundations using elastic theory and known or estimated soil elastic parameters Es and ν.

sections.title: Estimating Elastic Parameters, Es and ν
sections.summary: Covers estimation of soil elastic modulus (Es) and Poisson's ratio (ν) for mat/combined footing analysis. Discusses factors affecting Es (OCR, unit weight, moisture, disturbance), drainage-dependent modulus types (Es, E's, Eus), and provides typical values in Table 5-14, SPT/CPT correlations in Table 5-15 for coarse-grained soils, and OCR/PI correlation in Figure 5-30 for fine-grained soils. Eq. 5-38 relates ν to friction angle for drained conditions. Weighted averaging of Es over layered profiles is also addressed.
sections.body:
Accurately estimating the value of the soil modulus, Es, with depth below a combined footing or mat foundation can be challenging. The modulus tends to:
• Increase with increasing overconsolidation ratio (OCR),
• Increase with increasing unit weight,
• Decrease with increasing water content,
• Decrease in the laboratory compared to the field, and
• Decrease due to disturbance.

The soil modulus also depends on the drainage condition with Es used as general soil modulus, E's for drained soil modulus, and Eus for undrained soil modulus. These modulus values are much different than a true elastic material. In addition, the method of laboratory testing (confined, unconfined, drained, undrained) has an impact on the value of modulus. The values are typically defined using a secant method based on the stress and strain at a particular percentage of the ultimate strength. Typically, drained secant moduli are used for coarse-grained soils, and undrained secant moduli are used for fine-grained soils. Soil modulus values may be obtained from triaxial tests on undisturbed samples or in situ tests. The typical soil modulus values for all types of soil that are summarized in Table 5-14 should be used as a guide to check the validity of values from in situ or laboratory testing.

In coarse-grained soil, the value of E's varies with confinement. Thus, under a flexible mat foundation, the edges of the mat will deflect more than the center because the confinement is less at the edges. Also, the modulus increases with depth due to increased confining stress and increases during the application of load on the mat. In situ tests are preferred for estimating E's for granular soils due to disturbance issues with laboratory testing. Table 5-15 provides correlations of drained E's with SPT N and CPT qc values for coarse-grained soils.

For fine-grained soils, the undrained modulus usually increases with increasing vertical effective stress and undrained shear strength. The modulus also increases with OCR and lower moisture contents. Figure 5-30 provides a simple correlation between Eus, plasticity index (PI), and overconsolidation ratio (OCR). Once an appropriate ratio is selected, the undrained modulus can be estimated based on the undrained shear strength. Either in situ or laboratory tests are suitable for estimating Eus for fine-grained soils.

When layers with different soil properties underlie the mat, an appropriate weighted average Es must be determined. Within the depth of influence, the modulus of each layer can be multiplied by the layer thickness and summed. The weighted average is this sum divided by the total thickness. The depth of influence is usually assumed to be 2B and 4B for square and continuous foundations, respectively.

Typical values of Poisson's ratio, which is also required for an elastic analysis, are provided in Table 5-16. Note, ν is 0.5 for undrained conditions (i.e., no volume change ΔV = 0). For drained conditions, ν can be related to the friction angle:

ν = (1 − sin φ') / (2 − sin φ')  (5-38)

When φ' = 20° to 55°, the ν values range from 0.4 to 0.15.
key_points: Es increases with OCR and unit weight; decreases with water content and disturbance. Secant modulus at a fraction of ultimate strength is typically used.
Three modulus types: Es (general), E's (drained, for coarse-grained), Eus (undrained, for fine-grained).
Table 5-14 gives typical Es ranges; Table 5-15 provides SPT/CPT correlations for drained E's of coarse-grained soils. In situ tests preferred for granular soils.
For fine-grained soils, Eus correlates with PI and OCR via Figure 5-30; Eus also scales with undrained shear strength.
For layered profiles, compute depth-weighted average Es within 2B (square) or 4B (continuous) depth of influence.
Eq. 5-38 relates drained Poisson's ratio to friction angle: ν = (1 − sin φ') / (2 − sin φ'); φ' = 20°–55° gives ν = 0.15–0.4.
ν = 0.5 for undrained (no volume change) conditions; Table 5-16 provides typical ν values by soil type.

equations.description: Drained Poisson's ratio from friction angle: ν = (1 − sin φ') / (2 − sin φ'). For φ' = 20°–55°, ν ranges from 0.4 to 0.15.

figures: Figure 5-30 Undrained Modulus Correlation for Clay Soils with OCR and PI (after Duncan and Buchignani 1976)
tables: Table 5-15 Correlations for the Drained Modulus of Coarse-Grained Soils with SPT and CPT (after FHWA 2002a, Duncan and Bursey 2007, Coduto 2015, McGregor and Duncan 1998)
Table 5-16 Typical Values of Poisson's Ratio (after Bowles 1996)
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting elastic modulus (Es) and Poisson's ratio (ν) values for elastic settlement-based estimation of ks for mat or combined footing foundations in any soil type.

sections.title: Evaluation of ks for Time-Dependent Settlement
sections.summary: Covers how to incorporate time-dependent (consolidation) settlements into the subgrade modulus estimate for continuous footings or mat foundations. When imposed stresses exceed preconsolidation stress, or when recompression/heave occurs due to excavation, a reduced subgrade modulus (ksc) must be computed by adding consolidation settlement to elastic settlement, as expressed in Eq. 5-39.
sections.body: Time-dependent settlements must be included in the estimate for ks for a continuous footing or mat foundation when the structure imposes stresses beyond the preconsolidation stress, or when recompression or heave occurs due to excavation for the foundation. Neither of these settlements are included in the ks values estimated from Equation 5-35. In this case, consolidation settlement (sc) must be added to the elastic settlement, and the reduced subgrade modulus (ksc) is given by Eq. 5-39.
key_points: Time-dependent (consolidation) settlements are NOT included in ks values estimated from Eq. 5-35.
ksc (reduced subgrade modulus) must be used when stresses exceed preconsolidation stress or when recompression/heave occurs due to excavation.
ksc is computed by adding consolidation settlement (sc) to elastic settlement in the denominator of the subgrade modulus expression.
Eq. 5-39 provides the formulation for ksc incorporating both elastic and consolidation settlements.

equations.description: Reduced subgrade modulus (ksc) accounting for consolidation settlement: ksc = (ks · q0) / (q0 + sc/B · q/Es · (1 - μ²)), combining elastic and consolidation settlements in the denominator.

sections.applicability: Applies when designing continuous footings or mat foundations where imposed stresses exceed preconsolidation stress, or where recompression or heave occurs due to excavation.

sections.title: Iterative Process in Design
sections.summary: Describes the iterative design procedure required for mat foundations when non-uniform settlements or loading cause discrepancies between geotechnical and structural engineer estimates of contact pressures and settlements. The geotechnical engineer revises Es, ν, and ks/ksc values based on comparison with structural analysis until results converge. References Appendix B for an example mat design.
sections.body:
Although the contact pressures below a flexible mat are uniform for a uniform load, the settlements may vary across the mat because of variable stratigraphy. Also, the mat may not be uniformly loaded, and this will also cause settlements to be varied. Both of these nonuniformities can cause the design of a mat foundation to be an iterative process.

Contact pressures and settlements may be estimated by the structural engineer in the mat analysis, using the initial data provided by the geotechnical engineer including ksc. These should be compared to the contact pressures and settlements estimated by the geotechnical engineer. If they are substantially different, the geotechnical engineer should reevaluate the Es, ν, and ks or ksc values and settlements. Revised values should be provided to the structural engineer for the next iteration of modeling. The purpose is to make the settlements and contact pressures developed by the geotechnical engineer match closely with those of the structural engineer. An example mat design has been included in Appendix B.
key_points: Even under uniform loading, settlements across a mat can vary due to variable stratigraphy, requiring an iterative design approach.
Non-uniform loading also causes variable settlements, further necessitating iteration.
The geotechnical engineer provides initial Es, ν, and ks/ksc values; the structural engineer performs mat analysis and compares results.
If contact pressures and settlements differ substantially between the two engineers, the geotechnical engineer revises parameters for the next iteration.
Iteration continues until settlements and contact pressures from both disciplines are in close agreement.
An example mat design is provided in Appendix B.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing mat foundations subject to variable stratigraphy or non-uniform loading that causes differing settlement and contact pressure estimates between geotechnical and structural engineers.

sections.title: Node Coupling of Soil Effects
sections.summary: Explains how soil response is modeled at mat-soil interface nodes using the Winkler foundation concept in FEM/FGM software. Node spring stiffness K is computed as ks (or ksc) multiplied by the contributory area. Distinguishes between uncoupled and coupled springs, illustrating that uncoupled springs yield incorrect uniform settlements for flexible foundations, while coupled springs produce the correct dish-shaped deflection profile.
sections.body:
Mats are commonly designed using software that employs the FEM or FGM (ACI 2002). At the interface between the mat and the soil, the soil response is concentrated at nodes using a concept called a Winkler foundation. The soil is replaced by an equivalent spring with stiffness, K. The value of K for each node is determined by multiplying ks or ksc by the area (Acont) that contributes to the node (Eq. 5-40). The units of K are force per length. Figure 5-31 illustrates the procedure that is used to estimate K for various mat foundation contributary areas. The ks value assigned to each area shown in Figure 5-31 is based on the closest boring. A number of areas defined by the mat nodes may use the same ks value. This method produces uncoupled spring K values. An indirect method to allow coupling of nodes of Winkler foundations is discussed in the next section.

Uncoupled and coupled springs are illustrated in Figure 5-32. Uncoupling means that the settlement at any spring is unrelated to the settlement at any adjacent spring. The impact of coupling can be significant and can be seen for a uniformly loaded flexible foundation, such as a tank supported on clay. When the nodes are coupled, the deflection is correct and is dish shaped (concave). When uncoupled, the settlement is uniform and incorrect.

Coupling allows the responses at adjacent springs to affect each other. Coupling can also be accomplished when using a finite element computer program with the subgrade defined as an elastic medium, Es and ν, but this is seldom done because of the difficulty in programming and cost.
key_points: In FEM/FGM mat design, soil response at the mat-soil interface is modeled as Winkler foundation springs concentrated at nodes.
Node spring stiffness K = ks (or ksc) × contributory area (Acont); units are force per length (Eq. 5-40).
The ks value for each contributory area is assigned based on the closest boring; multiple areas may share the same ks.
This standard approach yields uncoupled springs: settlement at one node is independent of adjacent nodes.
Uncoupled springs produce incorrect uniform settlement for flexible foundations; coupled springs yield the correct concave (dish-shaped) settlement profile.
Coupling can be achieved by defining the subgrade as an elastic medium (Es and ν) in FEM, but this is rarely done due to programming difficulty and cost.

equations.description: Node spring stiffness for Winkler foundation: K = ks × Acont, where ks (or ksc) is the subgrade modulus and Acont is the contributory area at the node. Units of K are force per length.

figures: Figure 5-31 Computation of Uncoupled Winkler-type Soil Node Springs (after ACI 2002)
Figure 5-32 Coupled and Uncoupled Springs (after ACI 2002)
sections.applicability: Applies when modeling mat foundations using FEM or FGM software with Winkler-type soil springs to represent soil-structure interaction at the mat-soil interface.

sections.title: Indirect Method to Allowing Coupling
sections.summary: Describes Bowles (1996) indirect method for incorporating coupling effects in mat foundation analysis by zoning the mat with spatially varying subgrade modulus (ks) values. Uses Boussinesq vertical stress profiles at selected mat plan points and numerically integrated average stresses to compute reduced interior ks values relative to the edge ks, accounting for differential soil response across the mat.
sections.body:
Bowles (1996) suggested an indirect method for considering coupling in a mat foundation. This a structural consideration but is included herein to illustrate why this concept of coupling is important. The procedure is accomplished by selecting points on the mat plan so that the mat can be zoned with different values of ks. One point must be on the edge of the mat, and this must be assigned the ks value calculated for that location. The ks values on other interior points on the mat foundation are then reduced based on the edge ks using the procedure described in the following steps (see Figure 5-33):

1) Select sufficient points on the mat plan so that the mat can be zoned with different values of ks. See Points 1, 2, and 3 for a square mat in Figure 5-33. Point 1 is on the edge of the mat.
2) Select a depth of influence of 4B′ (B′ = the longest side of the mat and is unrelated to the usual depth of influence of 2B for square footings).
3) Plot vertical stress profiles for the square mat at points 1, 2, and 3 using the Boussinesq method (Figure 5-33b). For a square mat, 4B′ = 4B and q0 is the contact pressure.
4) Numerically integrate stress profiles to obtain the average vertical stress, σz,ave = (σz / qnet)·qnet. See Table 5-17.
5) These σz,ave are then designated σz,ave(1), σz,ave(2), and σz,ave(3) to correspond to Points 1, 2, and 3.
6) Compute ks for any point i as follows:

ks(i) = ks · [σz,ave(1) / σz,ave(i)]   (Eq. 5-41)

where: σz,ave(i) = average vertical stress at other points (Points 2 and 3 in Figure 5-33).

This procedure assumes an initial uniform ks value throughout the mat foundation. The example illustrates the difference between contributary areas and zones for the indirect method of allowing coupling. When ks values vary, as in the example in Figure 5-33 where Areas A, B, and C had different ks values, ks in Equation 5-39 varies with location. The procedure will reduce the ks values, but they will not be based on a uniform ks value as shown in the example of Figure 5-33. Table 5-17 contains estimated ksi values for different B′ / L ratios.
key_points: The indirect coupling method (Bowles 1996) zones the mat with spatially varying ks values rather than a single uniform value, capturing differential soil stiffness response.
One point must always be placed on the edge of the mat and assigned the ks calculated for that location; interior points receive reduced ks values.
Depth of influence for this method is 4B′ (longest mat side), distinct from the 2B rule used for individual square footings.
Boussinesq vertical stress profiles are plotted at each selected plan point and numerically integrated to obtain average vertical stress σz,ave.
Interior ks values are computed via Eq. 5-41: ks(i) = ks · [σz,ave(1) / σz,ave(i)], where Point 1 is the edge reference point.
The procedure reduces interior ks values relative to the edge but does not maintain a uniform ks baseline when zones A, B, and C differ.
Table 5-17 provides estimated ksi values for different B′/L ratios to support the numerical integration step.

equations.description: Subgrade modulus at interior point i: ks(i) = ks · [σz,ave(1) / σz,ave(i)], where σz,ave(1) is the average vertical stress at the edge reference point and σz,ave(i) is the average vertical stress at point i.

figures: Figure 5-33 Example Mat Foundation Indirect Coupling Problem
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or analyzing a mat foundation where coupling effects must be approximated by assigning spatially varying subgrade modulus values across different zones of the mat.

sections.title: Floating Mat Foundation
sections.summary: Explains the concept of a floating mat foundation, where the mat is sized so that the weight of excavated soil offsets the structural load, minimizing net settlement. Provides the formula for computing net bearing pressure (q_net) as the difference between total structural weight and weight of excavated soil divided by mat area, applicable when pressure distribution is uniform.
sections.body:
Depending on the structural geometry, weight, and load distribution on the mat, a mat foundation may float the structure in the soil, so that settlement only relates to recompression or heave. Where uniform, the pressure that results in settlement in a mat analysis can be computed as follows:

q_net = (W_structure - W_excavated) / A_mat

where:
W_structure = total weight of structure,
W_excavated = total weight of excavated soil, and
A_mat = area of mat.
key_points: A floating mat foundation is designed so the weight of excavated soil approximately balances the structural load, reducing net settlement.
Settlement in a floating mat is primarily due to recompression or heave rather than primary consolidation.
Net bearing pressure q_net = (W_structure − W_excavated) / A_mat, valid when pressure distribution is assumed uniform.
The concept applies when structural geometry, weight, and load distribution allow near-full compensation of overburden stress.

equations.description: Net mat bearing pressure: q_net = (W_structure - W_excavated) / A_mat, where W_structure is total structural weight, W_excavated is total weight of excavated soil, and A_mat is the area of the mat.

sections.applicability: Applies when designing a mat foundation intended to float a structure in soil, where uniform pressure distribution is assumed and settlement relates only to recompression or heave.

sections.title: Design for Special Loading Conditions
sections.summary: Introduces design of shallow foundations under special loading conditions, including high groundwater and uplift. Covers pressure-resistant vs. relieved foundation slabs and walls, uplift resistance via ground anchors and deadman systems, and transient uplift/moment loading on footings, piers, and posts.
sections.body: This section discusses the design of shallow foundations for special loading conditions. Design considerations for foundations and slabs to resist high groundwater are presented. Uplift resistance of shallow foundations is also considered.
key_points: Covers two major special loading topics: high groundwater resistance and uplift resistance for shallow foundations.
Distinguishes between pressure-resistant and relieved slab/wall systems based on groundwater depth and project economics.
Addresses uplift resistance via ground anchors (rock and soil), hydrostatic uplift design, transient loads on footings/piers/posts, and deadman anchors.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing shallow foundations subject to high groundwater, hydrostatic uplift, or transient uplift and moment loads.

sections.title: Pressure Resistant and Relieved Foundation Slabs and Walls
sections.summary: Covers hydrostatic pressure-resistant and relieved foundation slabs and walls, including when to use each system, dampproofing vs. waterproofing, drainage layer requirements, and the cutoff wall approach. Choice between systems depends on overall economy, maintenance, layout, and operation and must be evaluated project-by-project.
sections.body:
Hydrostatic pressure resistant and relieved foundation slabs and walls are considered in this section. Guidelines for the selection of appropriate drainage material are presented. Methods of dampproofing and waterproofing are also discussed.

Where the water table is deep, infiltration of surface water may still occur, and basement walls should be dampproofed. A drainage layer should be installed along walls with a foundation drain. A layer of drainage material should be placed under the slab with a vapor barrier.

Where the permanent water table is above the top of the basement slab, two general schemes are employed for basements. A pressure resistant slab and exterior foundation walls, pressure slab and walls, can be used. In this case, walls must be waterproofed to the maximum potential level of groundwater. Alternatively, the uplift pressures on the slab and the water pressure on walls can be relieved by a drainage system. This is referred to as a relieved slab and walls and requires dampproofing. In some cases, groundwater can be cut off by exterior foundation walls that extend into a low permeability thick clay layer or low permeability rock. In this case, a relieved slab is used and the exterior walls are waterproofed.

In general, the choice between pressure resistant or relieved slabs and walls depends on overall economy, maintenance, layout, and operation. This must be evaluated for each project individually.
key_points: When water table is deep, dampproof basement walls and install a drainage layer with vapor barrier under the slab.
When permanent water table is above basement slab, use either a pressure-resistant slab/wall system (waterproofed) or a relieved slab/wall system with drainage (dampproofed).
A cutoff wall extending into low-permeability stratum can reduce water flow/pressure, requiring waterproofing of exterior walls but allowing omission of wall drains.
Choice between pressure-resistant and relieved systems depends on economy, maintenance, layout, and operation and must be evaluated per project.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing basement foundations where the groundwater table may be at or above the basement slab elevation.

sections.title: Hydrostatic Pressure Slabs and Walls
sections.summary: Details design of pressure slabs to resist maximum probable hydrostatic uplift pressures, applicable for basements only slightly below groundwater. Specifies use of water-stops at construction joints, drainage layers with slotted PVC pipe, sumps, vapor barriers, and waterproofing of exterior walls to maximum anticipated groundwater level.
sections.body: For basements extending only a small depth below groundwater, a pressure slab to resist maximum probable hydrostatic uplift pressures may be economical. Water-stops should be provided at the construction joints, and a drainage layer should be installed between the pressure slab and floor slab to collect any leakage through the pressure slab. Drainage material should be as described in Section 5-5.1.3, and a slotted PVC corrugated drainage pipe should be added beneath the slab depending on the anticipated flow. A sump will be required to remove any water from the drainage layer. The exterior walls must be designed to withstand water pressure to the maximum anticipated level of ground water and must be waterproofed below this level. A vapor barrier should be placed over the drainage layer and under the slab to reduce the potential for moisture to migrate to the floor. An illustration of the pressure slab concept is shown in Figure 5-34.
key_points: Economical for basements only slightly below the groundwater table.
Water-stops required at all construction joints.
Drainage layer between pressure slab and floor slab collects leakage; slotted PVC corrugated pipe added based on anticipated flow.
Sump required to remove water from drainage layer.
Exterior walls must be waterproofed to maximum anticipated groundwater level.
Vapor barrier placed over drainage layer and under floor slab to limit moisture migration.
figures: Figure 5-34 Schematic of a Pressure Slab and Wall System
sections.applicability: Applies when designing basements that extend only a small depth below the groundwater table and a pressure-resistant slab system is selected.

sections.title: Relieved Slabs
sections.summary: Covers pressure relief design for basements at considerable depth below groundwater, including drainage layers at exterior walls and under floors, dampproofing requirements, and the cutoff foundation wall variant. Drainage layers, sumps, vapor barriers, and PVC drain pipes are key components; cutoff walls into low-permeability strata reduce required drainage infrastructure.
sections.body:
For basements at considerable depth below the groundwater level, it is usually economical to provide pressure relief along the foundation walls and beneath the floor slab. Drainage layers and drains are required at exterior walls and under floors to maintain no hydrostatic pressure on the walls or floor slab. Exterior walls below grade must be dampproofed. Additional dampproofing may be required on the interior of the basement walls depending upon the use.

If a thick, underlying stratum of low permeability clay or rock is relatively shallow, a cutoff foundation wall system may be economical. In this case, the foundation walls extend into the low permeability stratum and reduce water flow and pressures under the slab. Exterior walls below grade must be waterproofed, but wall drains may be omitted. Since some seepage may occur under the cutoff foundation walls, a drainage layer is required below the floor slab to maintain no hydrostatic pressure. Drain pipes are likely not needed due to low anticipated flow requirements. Additional dampproofing may be required on the interior of the basement walls depending upon the use.

Drainage material for relieved slabs should be as described in Section 5-5.1.3, and slotted PVC corrugated drain pipes may be needed beneath slab, depending on the anticipated flow. A sump is required to remove any water from the drainage layers. A vapor barrier should be placed over the drainage layer and under the slab to reduce the potential for moisture to migrate to the floor.
key_points: Economical for basements at considerable depth below the groundwater table.
Drainage layers and drains at exterior walls and under floors maintain zero hydrostatic pressure on slab and walls.
Exterior walls must be dampproofed; interior dampproofing may also be required.
Cutoff foundation walls extending into low-permeability stratum can eliminate wall drains and reduce drainage pipe requirements.
Cutoff wall variant requires waterproofing (not just dampproofing) of exterior walls.
Sump required; vapor barrier placed over drainage layer and under slab.
figures: Figure 5-35 Schematic of a Relieved Slab and Wall System
Figure 5-36 Schematic of a Cutoff Foundation Wall to a Low Permeability Stratum
sections.applicability: Applies when designing basements at considerable depth below the groundwater table where pressure relief via drainage is more economical than a pressure-resistant slab system.

sections.title: Underdrain System
sections.summary: Specifies materials and sizing for underdrain systems supporting relieved or pressure slab designs. Drainage material should be sound, clean gravel or crushed stone (3/4 to 2 inches), densified with a plate compactor. Slotted PVC corrugated pipes sized to anticipated flow discharge to a sump. Detailed filter and spacing guidance referenced from DM 7.1 Chapter 6.
sections.body: Drainage material should be sound, clean gravel or crushed stone graded between 3/4 and 2 inches. This material should be densified and leveled with a plate compactor. If needed, slotted PVC corrugated drainage pipes may be added beneath the slab and around the exterior walls. The pipes should be sized to carry the anticipated flow. The drainage material and pipes should flow to the sump for discharge. Drainage layer filter requirements and drain spacing are discussed in Chapter 6 of DM 7.1.
key_points: Drainage material: sound, clean gravel or crushed stone, 3/4 to 2 inches, densified with plate compactor.
Slotted PVC corrugated drainage pipes added beneath slab and around exterior walls as needed, sized to anticipated flow.
All drainage material and pipes must drain to the sump.
Filter requirements and drain spacing per DM 7.1, Chapter 6.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying underdrain systems beneath foundation slabs and along exterior walls for pressure-resistant or relieved slab designs.

sections.title: Dampproofing and Waterproofing Requirements
sections.summary: Defines dampproofing (resists moisture with no hydrostatic head) and waterproofing (resists water under hydrostatic pressure), and lists available systems including surface treatments, bitumen coatings, cementitious, hot-applied, and sheet/film membranes. Wall surfaces must be clean and dry before application. Table 5-18 enumerates methods.
sections.body: Dampproofing is defined as material that resists the passage of water with no hydrostatic pressure. Dampproofing is intended to keep soil moisture from entering a below grade space. A coating, usually asphalt-based, is either sprayed or hand applied to the outside of the wall. Dampproofing is not used when the groundwater level will be above a below grade space. Waterproofing is defined as material that resists the passage of water under hydrostatic pressure. A listing of dampproofing and waterproofing systems is provided in Table 5-18. Before application of dampproofing or waterproofing, all wall surfaces must be clean and dry and any defects corrected.
key_points: Dampproofing resists moisture passage with no hydrostatic pressure; typically asphalt-based, sprayed or hand-applied.
Dampproofing is NOT used when groundwater level will be above a below-grade space — waterproofing is required instead.
Waterproofing resists water passage under hydrostatic pressure.
Wall surfaces must be clean, dry, and free of defects before any application.

Available systems include surface treatments (silicates), bitumen/mastic asphalt, cement mortar, cementitious, hot-applied bitumen/rubberized asphalt, and film/sheet membranes (bentonite, HDPE, EPDM, PVC).
tables: Table 5-18 Methods of Foundation Dampproofing and Waterproofing
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and specifying dampproofing or waterproofing systems for below-grade foundation walls and slabs.

sections.title: Uplift Resistance
sections.summary: Introduces ground anchor design for uplift resistance, covering two failure mechanisms: individual anchor failure and group failure in a ground mass. Distinguishes passive (unprestressed) vs. active (prestressed) anchors. Active systems addressed include resistance to transient uplift on towers, sustained uplift on structures, and hydrostatic uplift forces. References FHWA (1999) for detailed guidance.
sections.body:
Ground anchors to resist uplift must be designed for two possible failure mechanisms: 1) failure of an individual anchor to resist the uplift load and 2) failure of a group of anchors in a ground mass where the total uplift load exceeds the capacity of the ground mass. In a group of anchors, the capacity of the group may be less than that of individual anchor times the number of anchors.

Anchors can be either passive or active. A passive anchor is one which is not prestressed and usually has no unbonded or free length. As load is applied, the anchor must move to engage resistance in the soil or rock. An active anchor is prestressed to a specific load and locked off. Active uplift anchor systems are considered herein and include: 1) resistance to transient uplift loads on tower legs, guys, and antennas, 2) sustained uplift loads on structures, and 3) structures impacted by hydrostatic uplift forces. Anchored systems, such as flexible anchored walls and soil nails have been discussed in Chapter 4. Landslide stabilization anchors are not considered. A brief discussion of corrosion protection is included at the end of this section. More detailed guidance for these subjects is found in FHWA (1999).

A ground anchor has multiple components as shown in Figure 5-37. A stressing anchorage and bearing plate connect the anchor to the structure. Anchors usually have an unbonded length that will transfer the load to soil or rock further from the structure. The final section of the anchor is the bond length where the resistance is developed. The load is transferred from the beginning of the anchor bond length and then progresses to the end of the anchor. Only a portion of the bond length is stressed under the allowable load. Ground anchors usually consist of deformed bars grouted in soil or rock. Tendons consisting of steel strand are also acceptable, and FHWA (1999) should be consulted for design. Bond stress may be increased by using washers or splayed bar ends. Spacers are used in angled holes to maintain the centrality of the bar in the anchor hole. The bond length and unbonded length should be grouted in one stage. This will help assure hole stability and provide continuous grout cover.
key_points: Design must address both individual anchor failure and group failure (group capacity may be less than sum of individual capacities).
Passive anchors move to engage resistance; active anchors are prestressed and locked off.
Active uplift systems cover transient loads (towers, guys, antennas), sustained structural uplift, and hydrostatic uplift.
Ground anchor components: stressing anchorage, bearing plate, unbonded length, and bond length.
Deformed bars grouted in soil or rock are typical; steel strand tendons are also acceptable per FHWA (1999).
Bond length and unbonded length should be grouted in one stage for hole stability and continuous grout cover.
figures: Figure 5-37 Schematic of Ground Anchor Components
sections.applicability: Applies when designing ground anchor systems to resist uplift forces on shallow foundations, including transient, sustained, and hydrostatic uplift scenarios.

sections.title: Rock Anchors
sections.summary: Covers design of ground anchors bonded into rock using rock mass breakout theory, which is conservative and best suited to weathered, severely fractured rock. Addresses four failure modes (cone breakout, grout/rock shear, grout/tendon shear, tendon tension), anchor spacing, bond length determination, presumptive bond stresses, corrosion protection classes, and load testing requirements.
sections.body:
Anchors are often bonded into rock. In most cases, local experience and knowledge should be relied upon to obtain the best anchor performance. As an alternative, the rock mass breakout theory presented in this section can be applied. It should be recognized that this theory is very conservative and is primarily applicable to weathered, severely fractured rock.

Rock mass breakout is resisted by the weight of the material above the bonded length. Four potential failure modes are considered in rock anchors that are often used to tiedown foundations:
• Failure from cone breakout of the rock mass
• Failure in shear along the grout/rock interface
• Failure in shear along the grout/tendon interface
• Failure of the tendon in tension

Design for these four failure modes is summarized in Figure 5-38. The required embedment or unbonded length is calculated based on the volume of the inverted cones above each anchor. The unbonded length (h) must be greater than 10 ft for bar anchors. When the anchor extends through soil before encountering rock, the cone diameter at the surface of rock is projected to the ground surface as a cylinder. The weight of the soil is included in the evaluation of h without considering the shear strength of the soil. Typically, the apex of the cone is placed at the top of the bond length of the anchor. The cone angle is typically assumed to fall between 60 to 90°, as shown in Figure 5-38(a), and is selected based on the quality of rock. This approach assumes that the rock is severely fractured and acts as a strong soil rather than an intact rock mass.

The spacing of rock anchors must consider the interference of cones shown in Figure 5-38(a). The depth will be greater if the spacing causes the cones to overlap since the volume of the individual cone will be less. This lowers the allowable capacity unless the unbonded length is increased. Spacing can also be constrained by structural stiffness issues and the presence of existing underground structures. If the anchor spacing is flexible, the spacing can be set as 2R, which causes the cones to touch but not overlap.

The anchor capacity will also be limited by the shear strength of the interface between the grout and the rock. For transient loads, a factor of safety of 2 to 3 is applied to the ultimate bond stress. For sustained loads, F of 3 is appropriate. The required anchor bond length (L) may be determined as shown in Figure 5-38(b). Presumptive ultimate bond stresses for various rock types are shown in Table 5-19. A lower factor of safety may be used for competent rock that is not highly fractured, and a higher factor of safety is required when highly weathered, fractured, or loose rock is engaged.

In weak rocks, such as mudstones and shales, rock anchor capacity is typically limited by the grout-rock interface. In strong, massive rock, the limiting failure mode may be at the grout-tendon interface as described in Figure 5-38(c), depending on the assumptions and construction methods. The allowable bond stress between the grout and tendon is typically assumed to be 10% of the unconfined compressive strength of the grout.

Finally, the tensile capacity of the tendon must be checked as described in Figure 5-38(d). The applied tensile stress should be calculated based on the applied load and the cross-sectional area of the tendon.

FHWA (1999) provides guidance on corrosion protection for ground anchors. Three levels of minimum corrosion protection are usually specified in U.S. practice:
• Class I protection – used for permanent anchors: unbonded length – bar surrounded with grease filled sheath within smooth bond breaker surrounded by grout and casing; bonded length – bar within grout-filled encapsulation surrounded by grout within soil or rock.
• Class II protection: unbonded length – bar surrounded with grease filled sheath surrounded with grout and casing; bonded length – grout surrounding bar within soil or rock.
• No protection for unbonded length and grout in bonded length.

Each ground anchor is load tested past the design load before putting it into service. About 2 percent of anchors are performance tested to 133 percent of the design load in a cycled test where 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, and 133 percent of the load is applied in steps and released. The load is then locked off at 75 to 100 percent of the design load. A hold is included in the performance test at 133 percent of design load to monitor creep movements. Every anchor that is not performance tested is proof tested to 125 percent of design load. This test is conducted in the same steps noted above, and the load is then locked off at 75 to 100 percent of the design load.
key_points: Rock mass breakout theory is conservative and best for weathered, severely fractured rock; local experience preferred where available.
Four failure modes: cone breakout, grout/rock shear, grout/tendon shear, tendon tension — all must be checked.
Minimum unbonded length (h) > 10 ft for bar anchors; cone angle 60–90° based on rock quality.
Anchor spacing should be ≥ 2R if flexible, to avoid cone overlap that reduces individual anchor capacity.
FS = 2–3 for transient loads; FS = 3 for sustained loads on grout/rock interface.
Allowable grout-tendon bond stress = 10% of grout unconfined compressive strength.
Performance test: 2% of anchors tested to 133% design load (cycled); all others proof tested to 125% design load; lock-off at 75–100% design load.
Three corrosion protection classes (Class I for permanent, Class II, and none) per FHWA (1999).

sections.title: Soil Anchors
sections.summary: Covers design of ground anchors in soil, noting that cone breakout is generally avoided by the minimum 10-ft unbonded length, so grout/soil interface shear typically governs. Provides presumptive ultimate bond stresses for fine-grained and coarse-grained soils, factors of safety for transient and sustained loads, and minimum anchor spacing of 5 ft.
sections.body:
Shallow anchors in soil have similar failure mechanisms as in rock: cone breakout and shear along the grout/soil interface. The cone breakout mechanism is typical for shallow anchors. However, if the minimum unbonded length of 10 feet for bars is used, it is generally not necessary to consider cone breakout. Soil anchors tend to be much deeper because the grout/soil interface bond stress is lower. Soil anchors with an uplift load are essentially micropiles with an uplift load. The minimum spacing between soil anchors should be 5 feet (Caltrans 2020). The appropriate inverted cone angle is in the range of 60 to 90°.

The design requirements shown in Figure 5-38 can also be used for soil anchors. The design should include selection of h, L, and tendon size. Presumptive ultimate bond stresses at the grout/soil interface for various soil types are shown in Table 5-20. Factors of safety of 2 and 3 can be used for transient and sustained loads, respectively, to calculate allowable bond stress. If the soil type changes along the anchor length, the side resistance can be divided into layers to allow the calculation of L.
key_points: Minimum unbonded length of 10 ft for bar anchors generally eliminates need to check cone breakout in soil.
Soil anchors are functionally similar to micropiles under uplift loading.
Minimum spacing between soil anchors: 5 ft (Caltrans 2020).
Inverted cone angle: 60–90°.
FS = 2 for transient loads; FS = 3 for sustained loads on grout/soil interface.
If soil type varies along anchor length, divide side resistance into layers to compute bond length L.
Presumptive bond stresses for soils range from 600 psf (soft lean clay) to 6,300 psf (dense glacial till).
figures: Figure 5-38 Ground Anchor Design Requirements
tables: Table 5-20 Presumptive Average Ultimate Bond Stress for Anchor Grout/Soil Interfaces with Gravity Grouting
sections.applicability: Applies when designing ground anchors bonded into soil to resist uplift forces, where grout/soil interface shear typically governs over cone breakout.

sections.title: Design of Anchors to Resist Hydrostatic Uplift
sections.summary: Addresses ground anchor design for resisting hydrostatic uplift forces, distinguishing between structures on rock/stiff soil and those on compressible soil with anchors in deeper layers. Requires verification that uplift (U) is resisted by structure weight (W1) plus enclosed soil mass weight (W2). Time-dependent anchor load changes from groundwater fluctuation, consolidation, and creep must be considered.
sections.body:
Ground anchors may also be used to provide resistance against uplift forces caused by hydrostatic pressures. Two cases can be considered: 1) the structure is founded on rock or relatively stiff soil or 2) the structure is founded on relatively compressible soil with the anchors secured in deeper soil or rock. When the structure is founded on rock or suitable soil for anchor development, the calculations presented in Section 5-5.2.2 and 5-5.2.3 can be used. When a more compressible soil layer exists between the structure and the anchors, as shown in Figure 5-40, changes in anchor loads resulting from movement of enclosed compressible ground mass (i.e., groundwater fluctuations, consolidation settlement or heave, or creep deformations) must be considered.

The design should verify that the hydrostatic uplift force (U) can be resisted by the weight of the structure (W1) plus the weight of the enclosed soil mass (W2). The uplift force should be calculated based on the maximum elevation of the water table. The buoyant unit weight of soils should be used for soils below the water table. Frictional resistance is neglected between the soil and walls of the structure. Friction is also neglected along the hypothetical vertical plane within the soil between the structure and the top of the bonded zone for the anchor (FHWA 1999).

The anchor loads can change with time. Groundwater fluctuations may cause cyclic changes in the anchor load. Consolidation and creep may result in detensioning. If any of these movements could cause additional tension in the tendons after lock-off, the tendons should be sized accordingly (FHWA 1999).
key_points: Two cases: structure on rock/stiff soil (use Sections 5-5.2.2/5-5.2.3) vs. structure on compressible soil with anchors in deeper strata (requires additional considerations).
Design must verify: U ≤ W1 (structure weight) + W2 (enclosed soil mass weight).
Uplift force based on maximum water table elevation; buoyant unit weight used for soils below water table.
Frictional resistance neglected between soil and structure walls, and along vertical planes between structure and anchor bond zone.
Anchor loads are time-dependent: groundwater fluctuations cause cyclic changes; consolidation and creep may cause detensioning.
Tendons must be sized to accommodate any additional tension that may develop after lock-off.
figures: Figure 5-40 Resisting Hydrostatic Uplift with Ground Anchors
sections.applicability: Applies when using ground anchors to resist hydrostatic uplift forces on structures, particularly where compressible soils exist between the structure and anchor bond zones.

sections.title: Transient Uplift Loads and Moments on Footings, Piers, and Posts
sections.summary: Addresses resistance of shallow foundations (footings, piers, posts) to transient uplift and moment loads. Simple design methods are presented in Figure 5-41. Moment loading design uses rigid retaining wall methods from Chapter 4. Detailed treatment of uplift and lateral loading for piers, posts, and piles is deferred to Chapter 6.
sections.body: Transient uplift and moment loads can be resisted by shallow foundations. Some simple methods to consider these loadings are presented in Figure 5-41. Design for moment loading can use methods for rigid retaining walls in Chapter 4. Uplift and lateral loading of piers, posts, and piles is addressed in more detail in Chapter 6.
key_points: Shallow foundations can resist transient uplift and moment loads using simplified methods.
Moment loading design may reference rigid retaining wall methods from Chapter 4.
Detailed guidance on uplift and lateral loading of piers, posts, and piles is in Chapter 6.
Figure 5-41 provides simplified design charts for footings, piers, and posts under transient uplift.
figures: Figure 5-41 Resistance to Transient Uplift Loads on Footings, Piers, and Posts
sections.applicability: Applies when designing shallow foundations (footings, piers, posts) to resist transient uplift and moment loads.

sections.title: Uplift Resistance Using a Deadman
sections.summary: Provides design guidance for concrete deadman anchors used to resist uplift forces. Notes that in weak soils, granular backfill replacement may be used and the passive wedge must be contained entirely within the granular fill. Design guidance and geometry are provided in Figure 5-42, with a caution to investigate stresses on remaining weak material.
sections.body: Guidance for the use of a concrete deadman for uplift resistance is provided in Figure 5-42. For a deadman in weak soil, it may be feasible to replace a considerable volume of soil with granular backfill and construct the block within the new backfill. If this is done, the passive wedge should be contained entirely within the granular fill, and the stresses on the remaining weak material should be investigated.
key_points: Concrete deadman anchors can provide uplift resistance for shallow foundations.
In weak soils, granular backfill replacement around the deadman may be feasible.
The passive wedge must be entirely contained within the granular fill zone.
Stresses on the remaining weak native material must be checked.
Design geometry and guidance provided in Figure 5-42.
figures: Figure 5-42 Design Guidance for Uplift Resistance by Concrete Deadman
sections.applicability: Applies when using a concrete deadman block to provide uplift resistance for a shallow foundation, particularly in weak soil conditions.

sections.title: Design for Special Soil Conditions
sections.summary: Container section covering foundation design in challenging soil environments including engineered fill, expansive soils and rock, collapsible soils, and other problem soil types. References subsections for detailed guidance on each condition and points engineers to Chapter 1 for a broader catalog of problem soil conditions.
key_points: Covers shallow foundation design in engineered fill, expansive soils, collapsible soils, and other problem soils.
Each subsection addresses identification, quantification of risk, and mitigation alternatives.
Regional experience is critical for identifying and addressing special soil conditions.
References DM 7.1, Chapter 5 for swelling computations and Chapter 1 for problem soil catalog.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing shallow foundations on non-standard or problematic soil conditions requiring special consideration beyond routine bearing capacity and settlement analyses.

sections.title: Shallow Foundations on Engineered Fill
sections.summary: Covers use of compacted structural fill to support structures and floor slabs, including its role in raising grade, replacing unsuitable soils, and providing a stiffer bearing mat. Emphasizes that fill design and field control must be directed by a geotechnical engineer, with additional detail referenced in Chapter 3.
sections.body: Engineered fill or compacted structural fill can be used to support structures and/or floor slabs. This fill is designed to have specific strength and compressibility properties and, as such, must be controlled in the field by personnel under the direction of a geotechnical engineer. Chapter 3 provides additional detail on fill compaction. Compacted structural fill is commonly used to raise the general grade for support of a structure. Structural fill may also be used beneath structures to allow for higher bearing pressures and reduce settlements by replacing unsuitable foundation soils and/or providing a relatively stiff mat of soil above less suitable soils.
key_points: Engineered fill must have designed strength and compressibility properties and be field-controlled by a geotechnical engineer.
Fill can raise general grade, replace unsuitable soils, or provide a stiff bearing layer above weak soils.
Higher-quality fill may allow higher bearing pressures and narrower foundations.
Chapter 3 provides additional detail on fill compaction requirements.
sections.applicability: Applies when compacted structural fill is used as the bearing material for shallow foundations or floor slabs.

sections.title: Compacted Structural Fill Requirements
sections.summary: Details design and monitoring requirements for compacted structural fill, including fill type selection, moisture content limits, subgrade evaluation, and construction specifications. Addresses compaction control testing, protection against wetting and frost, and references Section 5-2.5 for presumptive bearing pressures.
sections.body:
As noted in Chapter 3, compacted structural fill must be designed and monitored in order to provide adequate foundation support. Design of compacted fill includes selection of appropriate fill type by engineering classification and moisture content limitations. The suitability of subgrade for support of compacted structural fill should be evaluated by the subsurface exploration and field observations. Specifications for fill placement must be selected, including loose lift thickness, minimum relative compaction, and relative moisture content ranges. Section 5-2.5 provided presumptive bearing pressures for compacted fill.
During construction, structural fill should be monitored to determine if the material meets the classification and compaction requirements. Compaction control testing should verify that specifications have been met. Control tests should be checked for errors in testing or interpretation, such as degree of saturation greater than 100%. The fill should be protected against wetting by proper grading and surface drainage. In cold weather, a protective layer should be used to protect the surface from frost penetration.
key_points: Fill design requires selection of fill type by engineering classification and moisture content limits.
Subgrade suitability must be evaluated through subsurface exploration and field observations.
Specifications must define loose lift thickness, minimum relative compaction, and moisture content ranges.
Compaction control tests must be checked for errors (e.g., degree of saturation > 100%).
Fill must be protected from wetting (surface drainage) and frost (protective layer in cold weather).
Section 5-2.5 provides presumptive bearing pressures for compacted fill.
sections.applicability: Applies during design and construction monitoring of compacted structural fill intended to support shallow foundations.

sections.title: Geometric Limits of Compacted Structural Fill
sections.summary: Defines the required lateral and vertical extents of compacted structural fill under footings and for general grade raises. Specifies fill must extend at least 5 ft laterally beyond exterior footings or within a 1H:2V zone from footings. Addresses settlement analysis, subgrade stabilization needs, and when ground improvement or deep foundations may be required.
sections.body:
Where the general grade is raised for a structure, the entire building pad should be treated as compacted structural fill. The structural fill should extend laterally at least 5 ft outside the edge of the exterior footings or should encompass a zone extending downward at a 1H:2V angle from the footings, whichever is greater. More guidance on deep fills is provided in Section 3-6.5. In some cases, the upper few feet of a structural fill only support floor slabs and will have reduced compaction requirements.
Fill may also be used to replace unsuitable bearing soil. The vertical and lateral limits of the zone of compacted structural fill beneath footings should consider the vertical stresses imposed by the footings as shown in Figure 5-43. Unless adequate bearing soil is reached sooner, the excavation must extend to a depth that adequately reduces the change in stress from the foundation at the base of the fill. Continuous footings impose stresses to a greater depth than square footings with the same width. With high-quality fill, higher bearing pressures may allow narrower foundations that limit the depth of influence from individual foundations on the underlying soil.
Adequate bearing material may not be present within the depths indicated in Figure 5-43. In that case, the structural fill must be placed over underlying settlement prone material. The bottom of the excavation may require stabilization with geogrid or geotextile to allow fill to be placed and compacted. Alternatively, a bridging layer of gravel or cobble-sized material may be required. Settlement will likely control the net allowable bearing pressure for this situation. Settlement calculations should consider the increased stress on the underlying soil because of higher unit weight of the fill. Settlement may be caused by individual foundation loading as well as the combined change in stress from all of the building foundations. These should both be evaluated. If settlement cannot be mitigated, either ground improvement or deep foundation will likely be required.
key_points: Structural fill must extend at least 5 ft laterally beyond exterior footings, or within a 1H:2V downward zone from footings, whichever is greater.
Excavation depth must be sufficient to reduce foundation-induced stress to acceptable levels at the base of fill (see Figure 5-43).
Continuous footings stress the subgrade to greater depth than square footings of equal width.
If settlement-prone soils underlie fill, geogrid, geotextile, or a bridging layer may be needed at the excavation base.
Settlement analysis must account for both individual footing loads and combined building-wide stress increase, plus higher fill unit weight.
If settlement cannot be mitigated, ground improvement or deep foundations are required.
