sections.applicability: Applies when determining the required plan dimensions and depth of compacted structural fill zones beneath or around shallow footings.

sections.title: Foundations on Expansive Soil and Rock
sections.summary: Introduces expansive and swelling soils, their identification criteria (PI > ~20, low natural water content, arid or montmorillonite-bearing climates), and the climatic effects on heave vs. shrinkage behavior around foundations. Also flags sulfide-induced heave as a design consideration. References DM 7.1 Chapter 5 for heave computations and Section 1-2.12 for additional information.
sections.body:
Soils that undergo substantial or problematic volume changes upon wetting and drying are termed expansive or swelling soils. Surficial clays above the water table with a PI greater than about 20 and relatively low natural water content should be considered potentially expansive. These soils are most commonly found where the groundwater table is low in arid climates with a deficiency of rainfall and conditions of over-evaporation. Expansive soils are also found in more temperate climates where clay deposits are present that contain montmorillonite. Mottled, fractured, or slickensided clays, showing evidence of past desiccation, are particularly troublesome. For other causes of swelling in soils and for the computations of resulting heave see Chapter 5 of DM 7.1. Regional experience is critical for the identification of expansive soils and selection of foundation solutions. Additional information on these soils can be found in Section 1-2.12.
Climate has an important effect on the interaction between expansive soils and foundations. In arid regions, the soils tend to have a relatively low natural water content. Seasonal wetting tends to cause heave around the perimeter of structures and lifting of the edges of exterior foundations and slabs. In contrast, the soils in temperate climates tend to have a relatively high natural water content. Seasonal drying tends to cause shrinkage around the perimeter of structures. In this case, the exterior foundations and slab edges tend to drop or settle within time. These tendencies can affect the selection of appropriate mitigation alternatives for expansive soils.
Foundation design should also consider the potential for sulfide induced heave from soils and rock.
key_points: Soils with PI > ~20 and low natural water content above the water table should be considered potentially expansive.
Montmorillonite-bearing clays and mottled/slickensided/desiccated clays are particularly problematic.
Arid climates promote seasonal heave at structure perimeters; temperate climates promote seasonal shrinkage and edge settlement.
Climatic context affects which mitigation alternatives are most appropriate.
Sulfide-induced heave from soils and rock must also be considered in foundation design.
DM 7.1 Chapter 5 provides heave computation methods; Section 1-2.12 provides additional background.
sections.applicability: Applies when foundation soils are potentially expansive, swelling, or contain sulfidic materials that may cause volume change under moisture variation.

sections.title: Reducing Soil Expansion Potential
sections.summary: Presents three main strategies for reducing expansion potential: (1) removal and replacement with non-expansive compacted fill, (2) drilled shafts with underreams founded below the active swelling zone, and (3) relying on dead load to resist swell pressures with structurally supported slabs on cardboard forms. Details shaft design considerations for uplift forces from swelling soils.
sections.body:
Where economically feasible, remove potentially expansive soils from beneath footings and replace with compacted structural fill of non-expansive materials as shown in Figure 5-44(a). The fill should not allow water to collect or to be introduced to deeper expansive soils. Thus, low plasticity fine-grained soils are preferred. Alternatives to removal and replacement are discussed in the following paragraphs.
In some cases, column loads and floor loads with straight or underreamed drilled shafts founded below the zone of active swelling as illustrated in Figure 5-44(b). The soil along the upper part of the shaft will impart an upward force that must be resisted by the weight of the pier, the dead load, and the underreamed section. At any depth, the tensile force exerted on the shaft equals the shaft adhesion (see Chapter 6) times the difference in side area above and below the point under consideration. The reinforcement must resist these tensile forces and, if used, should extend into the underreamed section of the drilled shaft to allow engagement of the bell to resist uplift. An alternative is to place the shaft in an oversized hole and fill the annular space with a plastic material that can deform without developing adhesion to the shaft. Viscoelastic polymers, such as liquid rubber, are materials that fit this category. Placing the base of the foundation near the water table reduces heave damage because little change in moisture content occurs.
If the structure is sufficiently heavy and the soil is strong, the swell pressures can be resisted by the dead load of the structure. The floor slabs must be structurally supported overlying degradable cardboard forms as shown in Figure 5-44(c).
key_points: Preferred solution is removal and replacement with low-plasticity, non-expansive compacted fill that does not channel water to deeper expansive soils.
Drilled shafts with underreams founded below the active swelling zone can transfer loads below the problematic zone.
Upward tensile force on drilled shaft = shaft adhesion × difference in side area above and below the point; reinforcement must resist this.
Annular space between shaft and oversized borehole can be filled with viscoelastic polymer (e.g., liquid rubber) to prevent adhesion transfer.
Founding near the water table reduces heave because moisture content change is minimal.
Dead load of heavy structures can resist swell pressures; slabs should be on degradable cardboard forms to allow void space.
figures: Figure 5-44 Construction Details for Swelling Soils
sections.applicability: Applies when design requires active reduction of soil expansion potential beneath shallow foundations or floor slabs in expansive soil conditions.

sections.title: Minimizing Expansion Effects
sections.summary: Lists practical design and construction measures to minimize the structural effects of expansive soils when full removal is not economically feasible. Measures include compaction above optimum moisture, grade beams over cardboard, surface drainage, relocating utilities, lime/cement stabilization, and use of expansion joints in floor slabs.
sections.body:
Where it is not economically feasible to remove expansive materials or to support foundations below depths of possible expansion, the effects can be minimized by the following.
• Place fill with expansion prone plastic fines at moisture contents multiple percentage points above optimum moisture content at dry unit weight no higher than required for strength and compressibility.
• Construct grade beams over degradable cardboard.
• Provide impervious blankets or grade surface around structure to drain away from foundations.
• Locate water and drainage lines away from soils supporting foundations.
• Consider stabilization of the foundation soils with lime or cement to reduce the plasticity.
Where heave of the floor slab is not a critical concern, place concrete floor slabs directly on problem soil but provide expansion joints so the floor can move freely from structure.
key_points: Compacting expansive fill above optimum moisture at minimum required dry unit weight reduces future swell potential.
Grade beams should be constructed over degradable cardboard to allow soil movement without structural damage.
Surface grading and impervious blankets should direct water away from foundation soils.
Water and drainage lines should be kept away from foundation-bearing soils to prevent localized wetting.
Lime or cement stabilization can reduce soil plasticity and expansion potential.
Floor slabs can be placed on problem soils if expansion joints allow free movement relative to the structure.
sections.applicability: Applies when removal of expansive soils is not economically feasible and mitigation of structural effects through design measures is the preferred approach.

sections.title: Heave of Sulfide Soils and Rock
sections.summary: Addresses sulfide-induced heave and corrosion in foundations, describing the three forms of sulfur (sulfate, sulfide/pyritic, organic), identification and sampling protocols, heave potential thresholds (>0.1% pyritic sulfur), and mitigation for new and existing structures including removal, void fillers, sulfate-resistant cement, and sealing of remaining sulfidic material.
sections.body:
Foundation design should consider the potential for sulfide induced heave and corrosion. Sulfur may be present in sulfidic rock or soils below foundations or within compacted structural fill constructed of sulfidic rock or soils. The different forms of sulfur consist of (Dubbe 1984):
• Sulfate sulfur - represents a measure of the degree of oxidation and is an indication of the amount of expansion that has taken place before sampling;
• Sulfide (pyritic) sulfur - represents the amount of unoxidized sulfidic material and the potential expansion that can take place in the future; and
• Organic sulfur – represents material that is not believed to be involved in the expansive reaction.
Sulfide soil and rock is typically identified by testing. Samples of rock or soil for chemical testing of total sulfur forms should be wrapped in plastic to prevent any change in moisture content and to reduce oxidation before testing. Bryant et al. (2003) found that sulfide-induced heave can occur in materials containing as little as 0.1% sulfide [pyritic] sulfur. Figure 5-45 illustrates the potential for heave for various concentrations of sulfide [pyritic] sulfur.
Ground water should also be tested if it can rise to be in contact with foundations. Sulfide-induced corrosion of concrete can occur if sulfide (pyritic) sulfur exceeds 1200 ppm.
When testing indicates mitigation measures are warranted, the following should be considered:
• For new structures: remove sulfidic soil or rock below floor slab and/or footings unless dead loads are sufficient to prevent heave and use void filler below grade beams and slabs as discussed for expansive soils;
• For protection of concrete subject to sulfidic groundwater use: 1) sulphate resistant cement such as Type V Portland cement, 2) lower water-cement ratio concrete, or 3) coat concrete with bitumen; and
• For existing structures consider partial or complete removal of sulfidic soil or rock below floor slab and/or footings depending upon how heave has impacted the structure.
If testing indicates oxidation is complete and damage has already occurred, the sulfidic soil or rock does not need to be removed. Partial excavation and replacement can be used if necessary but any sulfidic material left in place below the structure should be completely covered with spray mastic to seal the area from air. The excavated areas should be backfilled with structural fill that is below problematic levels for sulfur. Flowable fill has also been used as backfill.
Electrical corrosive properties of soil are important where metal structures such as pipelines, etc. are buried underground. A resistivity survey of the site may be necessary to evaluate the need for cathodic protection.
key_points: Sulfide (pyritic) sulfur represents future expansion potential; sulfate sulfur indicates oxidation already occurred; organic sulfur is not expansive.
Samples for sulfur testing must be wrapped in plastic immediately to prevent oxidation before testing.
Heave can occur at pyritic sulfur content as low as 0.1%; concrete corrosion risk when sulfide sulfur exceeds 1200 ppm in groundwater.
New structure mitigation: remove sulfidic material or use void fillers; protect concrete with Type V cement, low w/c ratio, or bitumen coating.
Existing structure mitigation: partial/complete removal of sulfidic material; remaining material must be sealed with spray mastic to prevent air contact.
Site resistivity survey may be needed to assess cathodic protection requirements for buried metal structures.
figures: Figure 5-45 Potential Sulfidic Rock Heave (after Bryant et al. 2003)
sections.applicability: Applies when foundation soils or rock, or compacted fill materials, may contain sulfidic (pyritic) minerals capable of causing heave or concrete corrosion.

sections.title: Foundations on Collapsible Soils
sections.summary: Introduces collapsible soils — their metastable structure, collapse mechanism upon inundation, typical deposit types (loess, debris flows, loose fills, decomposed igneous rock), global distribution, and factors affecting collapse magnitude. Notes deposits can exceed 500 ft depth and that large settlements can result. References Section 1-2.3 for additional loess information.
sections.body:
Collapsible soils are characterized by a metastable structure and undergo an abrupt collapse when they are inundated. Thus, existing deposits are located above the water table in their natural state. Most collapsible soils are either debris flow deposits of low unit weight or wind deposits (loess). Loose fills and decomposed igneous rocks can also be collapsible. They usually consist of silts and sands with a substantial fines content. Additional information on loess is found in Section 1-2.3.
Collapsible soils are located in the Midwest and Southwest United States, parts of Asia, South America, and Southern Africa according to Mitchell and Soga (2005). The geographic location of loess deposits in the United States, South America, Europe, and Asia are shown in Figure 5-46. The depth of collapsible soil deposits can be very great, often up to 100 ft and sometimes over 500 ft (USBR 1992). Because of the substantial thickness, large settlements can result from collapse. USBR (1992) also stated that the amount of collapse is affected by layer thickness, soil mineralogy, initial void ratio, stress history, grain shape, moisture content, pore sizes, any cementing agents, and the amount of added load (hydrostatic or structural).
key_points: Collapsible soils have metastable structure and collapse abruptly upon inundation; they exist above the water table in natural state.
Most common types are loess (wind deposits) and debris flow deposits; also includes loose fills and decomposed igneous rock.
Deposits can reach over 500 ft depth, leading to potentially very large settlements.
Collapse magnitude depends on layer thickness, mineralogy, void ratio, stress history, grain shape, moisture, pore size, cementing agents, and applied load.
Found in Midwest and Southwest US, parts of Asia, South America, and Southern Africa.
figures: Figure 5-46 Loess Distribution – (a) United States, (b) South America, (c) Europe, and (d) Asia (after Muhs 2013)
sections.applicability: Applies when foundation sites may overlie loess, debris flow deposits, loose fills, or other collapsible soil types, particularly in arid or semi-arid regions.

sections.title: Identification of Collapsible Soils
sections.summary: Describes the four key tasks for working with collapsible soils and the screening method using natural dry unit weight plotted against liquid limit (Figure 5-47) to identify potentially collapsible soils. Notes that rising groundwater is the only method ensuring 100% saturation and that undisturbed sampling of silts and fine sands is challenging.
sections.body:
The following tasks need to be accomplished when working with collapsing soils (Houston et al. 2001):
• Identification and characterization of collapsible soil sites,
• Estimation of the extent and degree of wetting when collapse occurs,
• Estimation of collapse settlements, and
• Selection of design and mitigation alternatives.
Estimation of the extent and degree of wetting required for collapse is the most difficult of these tasks. Rising groundwater is the only method that will ensure 100 percent saturation. Irrigation from the surface will not usually result in 100 percent saturation.
The most danger occurs when these soils are not identified, and a structure is damaged due to soil collapse. As a simple test to identify collapsible soils, the natural dry unit weight of a soil sample can be plotted against the liquid limit on Figure 5-47 (USBR 1992). The curves represent the dry unit weight corresponding to a saturated soil with a water content equal to the liquid limit. If the natural dry unit weight is lower than the saturation line, the soil is potentially collapsible. The most difficult problem with this identification test is obtaining undisturbed samples for testing. Undisturbed sampling of silts and fine sands is difficult, and disturbance will impact the results. Many collapsing soils will slake upon immersion, but this is not a definitive indicator.
key_points: Four required tasks: identification, degree-of-wetting estimation, settlement estimation, and mitigation selection.
Rising groundwater is the only mechanism ensuring 100% saturation; surface irrigation typically achieves only partial saturation.
Screening tool: plot natural dry unit weight vs. liquid limit — if below the saturation curve (Figure 5-47), soil is potentially collapsible.
Undisturbed sampling of silts and fine sands is difficult and disturbance affects identification test results.
Slaking upon immersion is common in collapsible soils but is not a definitive identification indicator.
figures: Figure 5-47 Criteria for Evaluation of Collapsing Soils (after USBR 1992)
sections.applicability: Applies during site investigation and initial characterization of potentially collapsible soil deposits.

sections.title: Estimated Degree of Wetting When Collapse Occurs
sections.summary: Discusses wetting conditions required for collapse, noting that full collapse requires a rising water table while partial collapse can occur from irrigation (35–60% saturation). References ASTM D4546 for full-wetting collapse testing and notes ASTM D5333 (collapse index) has been withdrawn.
sections.body: Houston et al. (2001) indicate that full collapse only occurs in the field with a rising water table, but partial collapse can occur at moisture contents less required for 100 percent saturation, such as from irrigation. Typical saturation levels achieved during irrigation are 35 to 60 percent. Full wetting collapse is usually identified in the laboratory using one-dimensional consolidation tests in accordance with ASTM D4546.
key_points: Full collapse requires a rising water table achieving near-100% saturation.
Partial collapse can occur from irrigation, which typically achieves only 35–60% saturation.
Full wetting collapse is characterized in the laboratory using 1D consolidation tests per ASTM D4546.
ASTM D5333 (collapse index method) has been withdrawn from use.
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating whether site wetting conditions (rising water table vs. surface irrigation) will produce full or partial collapse of collapsible soils.

sections.title: Estimation of Collapse Settlements
sections.summary: Describes use of 1D consolidation tests to quantify collapse potential and collapse index, summarized in Table 5-21. Explains how strains from inundation tests (ASTM D4546) are multiplied by layer thickness to estimate settlement, with caution about non-uniform field wetting. Notes that in seismic areas, further collapse/densification may occur post-mitigation.
sections.body:
One-dimensional consolidation tests can be used to determine two different qualitative measures of collapse. The collapse potential is the strain caused by wetting at any stress level while the collapse index is the relative collapse for inundation at a stress of 4000 psf (ASTM D5333, Jennings and Knight 1975). Relative classification of collapse associated with these two measures are summarized in Table 5-21.
The magnitude of collapse can be estimated using the results of one-dimensional tests on one or more specimens inundated at vertical stress conditions applicable to the project conditions (ASTM D4546). The strain caused by wetting is directly measured for each specimen and used to estimate strain under field conditions. Because close to full saturation is achieved, the strains measured in the laboratory tests tend to be conservative compared to typical field wetting. Boundary conditions and nonuniformity in field conditions can make the laboratory measured rates of collapse unreliable (ASTM D4546).
Settlement caused by collapse can be estimated by multiplying the decimal strain by the thickness of the soil layer. If multiple collapse tests are performed at different vertical stresses, the settlement can be predicted for each layer and summed.
In earthquake prone areas, densification and collapse may occur even after mitigation and should be evaluated (Houston et al. 2001). For example, prewetting may only cause partial wetting collapse, and the soil may still be subject to densification by earthquake shaking.
key_points: Collapse potential = strain at wetting under any stress; collapse index = relative collapse at 4000 psf inundation (per ASTM D5333, now withdrawn).
Settlement = decimal strain × layer thickness; sum contributions from each layer when multiple tests are performed.
Laboratory tests are conservative (near-full saturation) vs. typical field wetting; boundary/nonuniformity effects can make lab rates unreliable.
In seismic zones, prewetting may only partially collapse soils, leaving residual densification potential from earthquake shaking.
Table 5-21 classifies collapse severity from None to Severe based on both measures.
tables: Table 5-21 Classification of Collapse (after ASTM D 5333, Jennings and Knight 1975)
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating collapse settlement magnitudes for collapsible soil deposits using laboratory consolidation test data.

sections.title: Mitigation Alternatives
sections.summary: Lists and evaluates available mitigation methods for collapsible soils: removal and replacement (most common, best for shallow depths), avoidance of wetting, deep dynamic compaction, chemical stabilization/grouting, deep foundations, and prewetting. Notes that prewetting is less successful when little additional load is applied during wetting.
sections.body:
Available mitigation alternatives for collapsible soils include:
• Removal and replacement with compacted structural fill,
• Avoidance of wetting,
• Deep dynamic compaction,
• Chemical stabilization or grouting,
• Deep foundations, and
• Prewetting.
The most widely used mitigation method is removal and replacement with compacted structural fill. Often the excavated material is reused as fill. For shallow depths of collapsible material, this is the least costly and best alternative. Avoidance of wetting has also been used where slopes are used to divert water away from the structure. Prewetting is less successful where little additional load is applied during wetting.
key_points: Removal and replacement with compacted structural fill is the most widely used and cost-effective method for shallow collapsible deposits.
Excavated collapsible material is often reused as compacted fill after removal.
Avoidance of wetting (surface grading/slopes) is a viable alternative where water diversion is achievable.
Prewetting is less effective when little additional structural load is applied during the wetting process.
Deep dynamic compaction, chemical stabilization/grouting, and deep foundations are also available mitigation options.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting remediation or mitigation strategies for shallow foundations bearing on or near collapsible soil deposits.

sections.title: Other Problem Soils
sections.summary: Provides a tabular reference (Table 5-22) summarizing primary shallow foundation design considerations for soft clays/organics/peat, stiff fissured expansive clays/shales, loess/collapsible soils, sensitive clays, residual soils, laterites, and talus. Points to Chapter 1 for a comprehensive catalog of problem soil conditions.
sections.body: Chapter 1 provides a summary of many types of problem soil conditions that can affect the design of foundations and earth structures. Table 5-22 summarizes important conditions for the design of shallow foundations in problem soils.
key_points: Table 5-22 consolidates primary shallow foundation considerations for seven major problem soil types into a single reference.
Soft clays, organics, peat, and muskeg: low allowable bearing, secondary compression critical, often requires ground improvement or deep foundations.
Stiff fissured clays/shales: shrink/swell potential controls design; bearing capacity rarely critical except for very high loads.
Sensitive clays: shear stress must not exceed peak shear strength; eccentrically loaded foundations must use maximum bearing pressure for FS calculation.
Residual soils: standard correlations may be unreliable; coefficient of compressibility preferred for settlement.
Laterites: weakly cemented types may fail under cyclic loads or flowing groundwater.
Talus: global stability must be assessed before use as shallow foundation support.
tables: Table 5-22 Problem Soil Considerations for Shallow Foundations
sections.applicability: Applies as a quick-reference guide when evaluating shallow foundation design in any of seven recognized problem soil categories.
